title: Robust quantum obfuscation under implementation error
subfield: Quantum indistinguishability obfuscation
open: Can quantum indistinguishability obfuscation retain its security guarantees when the obfuscated functionality is implemented only approximately, subject to small diamond-norm error? The target is a robustness statement that survives entangled auxiliary inputs and repeated composition of the obfuscated object, not merely closeness to the exact channel functionality.
status: The exact channel functionality achieved by known obfuscation does not establish this fault-tolerant robustness statement; the question remains open, with connections to fault-tolerance thresholds and continuity bounds for quantum channels. Key work: Huang–Tang (2026), *Obfuscation of Arbitrary Quantum Circuits*, arXiv:2601.08969.
solved_when: A construction of quantum indistinguishability obfuscation is given whose security is provably stable under small diamond-norm implementation error, including the presence of entangled auxiliary inputs and under repeated composition.
why: Physical quantum gates never implement ideal channels exactly, so an obfuscation scheme whose security proof assumes exact channel functionality cannot be deployed on real hardware.
key_works: Huang–Tang (2026), *Obfuscation of Arbitrary Quantum Circuits*, arXiv:2601.08969.

bib.title: Robust quantum obfuscation under implementation error

title: Complete fault-tolerant resource estimates for quantum iO
subfield: Quantum indistinguishability obfuscation
open: Can we produce a complete fault-tolerant resource estimate for an explicit candidate construction of quantum indistinguishability obfuscation, detailing what it would physically take to run such an obfuscator on real quantum hardware?
status: Existing constructions are in the oracle model and do not provide a complete physical implementation record; see Bartusek et al. (2025/2026), *Classical Obfuscation of Quantum Circuits via Publicly-Verifiable QFHE*, arXiv:2510.08400.
solved_when: A full physical implementation record exists for an explicit quantum-obfuscation candidate, specifying logical-qubit counts, non-Clifford gate costs, memory lifetimes, and error budgets.
why: It would reveal whether computation, storage, or error correction is the dominant obstacle to realizing quantum iO.
key_works: Bartusek et al. (2025/2026), *Classical Obfuscation of Quantum Circuits via Publicly-Verifiable QFHE*, arXiv:2510.08400.

title: QMA witness encryption under conventional assumptions
subfield: Quantum indistinguishability obfuscation
open: Can we build an encryption scheme for QMA instances such that anyone holding an appropriate quantum witness can decrypt, under conventional assumptions — and can the scheme offer an explicit consumable-witness or reusable-witness functionality?
status: Recent barriers distinguish the ciphertext and reduction models used to attack this problem, but they do not rule out every quantum-state construction. Key work: Barhoush–Morimae–Movassagh (2026), ePrint 2026/1800.
solved_when: A construction exists that encrypts relative to arbitrary QMA instances, permits decryption given a quantum witness (consumed or reusable as specified), and rests on conventional assumptions; no quantitative budgets are stated beyond this functional criterion.
why: It would let possession of quantum evidence serve as a cryptographic access condition, turning verifiable quantum proof into a decryption key.
key_works: Barhoush–Morimae–Movassagh (2026), ePrint 2026/1800.

bib.title: QMA witness encryption under conventional assumptions

title: Function-hiding general FE from lattices
subfield: Functional encryption for general circuits
open: Can we construct functional encryption for general circuits, from plain lattice assumptions, that hides both the encrypted data and the program embedded in each functional key, aside from whatever the decrypted outputs inherently reveal? More precisely, the goal is a lattice-based construction achieving function privacy for general circuits modulo unavoidable output leakage.
status: Known constructions handle restricted function families, and generic-group barriers (Hajiabadi–Langrehr–Wang, 2026, *Generic-Group Barriers for Function-Hiding and Multi-Input Functional Encryption*, ePrint 2026/1149) rule out certain approaches, but together these do not settle function hiding for general circuits over lattices.
solved_when: A construction (or a matching impossibility) is given for general-circuit functional encryption from plain lattice assumptions that achieves function hiding up to output leakage.
why: Such a scheme would protect proprietary models and queries — the functionality being evaluated — in addition to the input data, which current functional encryption leaves exposed.
key_works: Hajiabadi–Langrehr–Wang (2026), *Generic-Group Barriers for Function-Hiding and Multi-Input Functional Encryption*, ePrint 2026/1149.

title: The attainable simulation-security map for FE
subfield: Functional encryption for general circuits
open: Which notions of simulation-based security for general functional encryption are actually attainable when keys may be requested adaptively, multiple challenge messages are encrypted, the functionality leaks output information, and the simulator is given bounded resources? A full answer would map the space of simulation definitions, showing exactly which combinations of these parameters are realizable and which fall into the known impossible regimes.
status: Indistinguishability security is known not to imply every simulation formulation, and work on randomized functionalities (Datta–Guan–Korb–Sahai (2025), *(Multi-Input) FE for Randomized Functionalities, Revisited*, ePrint 2025/330) exposes important definitional gaps, but no complete map of the attainable simulation-security regimes is known.
solved_when: A characterization exists that, for every combination of adaptive key requests, multiple challenge messages, output leakage, and simulator resource bounds, either gives a construction achieving that simulation notion or an impossibility proof ruling it out — and the characterization respects all previously established impossibility results.
why: It separates privacy promises a general-circuit FE scheme can meaningfully make from definitions that no scheme can satisfy, giving cryptographers a definitive reference for which simulation notions to target and which to abandon.
key_works: Datta–Guan–Korb–Sahai (2025), *(Multi-Input) FE for Randomized Functionalities, Revisited*, ePrint 2025/330.

bib.title: The attainable simulation-security map for FE

title: Strong randomized MIFE without subexponential iO
subfield: Functional encryption for general circuits
open: Can we build adaptively secure randomized multi-input functional encryption, robust against both malicious encryptors and malicious decryptors, while assuming only polynomial-strength indistinguishability obfuscation (or avoiding subexponential iO altogether)? In other words, is subexponential hardness of iO truly necessary for this level of security and functionality?
status: The Datta–Guan–Korb–Sahai (2025) construction *(Multi-Input) FE for Randomized Functionalities, Revisited* (ePrint 2025/330) supports unbounded messages per slot under subexponential iO; that functionality itself is no longer the open question — the gap is the assumption.
solved_when: A construction of adaptive randomized multi-input FE secure against malicious encryptors and decryptors is given, with security reducing to iO (or other assumptions) of polynomial — not subexponential — hardness.
why: Randomness in the functionality must not become a covert channel leaking secrets; removing the subexponential assumption would place strong randomized MIFE on standard, plausible hardness.
key_works: Datta–Guan–Korb–Sahai (2025), *(Multi-Input) FE for Randomized Functionalities, Revisited*, ePrint 2025/330.

bib.title: Strong randomized MIFE without subexponential iO

title: Compact FE with many corrupted authorities
subfield: Functional encryption for general circuits
open: Can decentralized multi-authority functional encryption for general circuits remain secure when many authorities are corrupted? In particular, is there a construction with compact parameters tolerating more than logarithmically many corrupted authorities, without assuming general indistinguishability obfuscation?
status: The 2026 revision (Goyal–Yadugiri, 2025/2026; ePrint 2025/412) identifies an iO implication for sufficiently compact regimes with high corruption, showing those regimes cannot be settled without essentially reaching obfuscation; existing limited-corruption constructions do not resolve the compact, many-corruption setting.
solved_when: A decentralized multi-authority FE scheme for general circuits is given whose parameters are compact and which tolerates more than logarithmically many corrupted authorities, with security proved without assuming general iO.
why: Without such a scheme, decentralization loses its point as soon as the number of compromised authorities grows; a solution keeps the trust model meaningful precisely when many authorities collude or fall.
key_works: Goyal–Yadugiri (2025/2026), ePrint 2025/412.

bib.title: Compact FE with many corrupted authorities

title: Dynamic decentralized FE with composable authority changes
subfield: Functional encryption for general circuits
open: Can decentralized multi-authority functional encryption for general circuits be extended to a setting where the set of authorities itself changes over time — authorities join, depart, are compromised, and recover — while preserving ciphertext validity and preventing cross-epoch key substitution?
status: Static authority guarantees, such as those in Goyal–Yadugiri (2025/2026), *Decentralized Multi-Authority Functional Encryption with Malicious Authorities*, ePrint 2025/412, do not by themselves establish this lifecycle functionality.
solved_when: A construction (with proof) exists that supports authority joins, departures, compromise, and recovery while preserving ciphertext validity across epochs and preventing cross-epoch key substitution.
why: Real access-control systems change membership over years, so a scheme whose guarantees hold only for a fixed authority set cannot be deployed; this would make decentralized FE usable for long-lived dynamic organizations.
key_works: Goyal–Yadugiri (2025/2026), *Decentralized Multi-Authority Functional Encryption with Malicious Authorities*, ePrint 2025/412.

bib.title: Dynamic decentralized FE with composable authority changes

title: Large-domain MCFE from minimal assumptions
subfield: Functional encryption for general circuits
open: Can multi-client functional encryption for general circuits be built from minimal assumptions over exponentially large input domains, without the ciphertext or key material blowing up exponentially with the domain size?
status: The current state of the art is the 2025–2026 small-domain result of Biswas–Vaid–Yerukhimovich (*Multi-Client Functional Encryption for Small Domains*, ePrint 2025/2210), which comes with domain, arity, and query-bound qualifications; no large-domain extension from minimal assumptions is known.
solved_when: A construction extending minimal-assumption small-domain MCFE to exponentially large domains exists with only polynomial (non-exponential) encoding expansion.
why: Long records, identifiers, and numerical encodings naturally require large domains, so small-domain constructions alone cannot serve realistic data.
key_works: Biswas–Vaid–Yerukhimovich (2025/2026), *Multi-Client Functional Encryption for Small Domains*, ePrint 2025/2210.

title: Tensor-preimage-hint security from ordinary LWE
subfield: Restricted FE, attribute-based encryption, and registration
open: Can the higher-degree tensor-preimage-hint assumption underlying polynomial functional encryption be derived from ordinary LWE — or is there an attack that separates it from LWE? Formally, one asks for a reduction from (or a distinguishing attack against) the tensor-preimage-hint assumption at degrees above one to the standard Learning with Errors problem.
status: The 2026 construction of Cini–Lai–Ünal–Woo (*Lattice-based Secret-Key Functional Encryption for Constant-Degree Polynomials*, ePrint 2026/1977) reduces the degree-one case to LWE, but higher degrees require a new assumption.
solved_when: Either a proof reduces the higher-degree tensor-preimage-hint assumption to ordinary LWE, or a separating attack is exhibited that breaks the assumption under LWE hardness.
why: A reduction would give polynomial functional encryption for low-degree polynomials a standard-assumption foundation; a separation would show the current constructions rest on an assumption genuinely stronger than LWE.
key_works: Cini–Lai–Ünal–Woo (2026), *Lattice-based Secret-Key Functional Encryption for Constant-Degree Polynomials*, ePrint 2026/1977.

title: Public-key quadratic FE from plain LWE
subfield: Restricted FE, attribute-based encryption, and registration
open: Can we build a public-key functional encryption scheme for general quadratic functions, secure against unbounded collusion, from the plain Learning with Errors assumption, with polynomial-size parameters? Formally, the goal is an unbounded-collusion public-key FE scheme for the class of all quadratic functions whose security reduces to standard LWE and whose master keys, ciphertexts, and keys have polynomial size.
status: Existing candidates for low-degree functional encryption in the lattice setting are secret-key only (Cini–Lai–Ünal–Woo (2026), *Lattice-based Secret-Key Functional Encryption for Constant-Degree Polynomials*, ePrint 2026/1977), and these do not establish the public-key, plain-LWE target sought here.
solved_when: A construction of public-key FE for general quadratic functions is given, secure against unbounded collusions, based on the ordinary LWE assumption, with all parameters (keys, ciphertexts, function keys) of polynomial size.
why: Quadratic functions already capture covariance, similarity, and many other statistical computations, so such a scheme would give a standard-assumption route to privacy-preserving statistics on encrypted data.
key_works: Cini–Lai–Ünal–Woo (2026), *Lattice-based Secret-Key Functional Encryption for Constant-Degree Polynomials*, ePrint 2026/1977.

bib.title: Public-key quadratic FE from plain LWE

title: Adaptive constant-degree lattice FE
subfield: Restricted FE, attribute-based encryption, and registration
open: Can the selective-security constant-degree lattice functional encryption candidate be made adaptively secure without prohibitive security loss or stronger assumptions?
status: The 2026 construction of Cini–Lai–Ünal–Woo (EPrint 2026/1977) remains selective-secure, and that qualification remains substantive; no adaptive-security upgrade is known.
solved_when: A constant-degree lattice FE construction is proven adaptively secure under the same assumptions as the 2026 selective-secure candidate, with security loss that is not prohibitive.
why: Users choose later computations after observing earlier outputs, so selective security does not capture the realistic adaptive setting.
key_works: Cini–Lai–Ünal–Woo (2026), ePrint 2026/1977.

title: Compact post-quantum function-hiding quadratic FE
subfield: Restricted FE, attribute-based encryption, and registration
open: Can quadratic functional encryption be made simultaneously function-hiding, compact, and post-quantum secure — without inflating quadratic evaluations into high-dimensional inner-product computations that destroy compactness? More precisely: construct function-hiding FE for quadratic functions with compact ciphertexts/keys from post-quantum assumptions.
status: Function hiding, quadratic expressiveness, and compactness are currently separate requirements that have not been achieved together, and generic-group barriers (Hajiabadi–Langrehr–Wang (2026), *Generic-Group Barriers for Function-Hiding and Multi-Input Functional Encryption*, ePrint 2026/1149) constrain simple extensions. Related directions include low-rank representation and private kernel methods.
solved_when: A construction is given that achieves function hiding, quadratic expressiveness, and compactness at once, under post-quantum assumptions, without reduction to inner-product FE in expanded dimensions.
why: It would let a cloud evaluate useful statistical models (naturally quadratic) while protecting both the model and the inputs it is evaluated on.
key_works: Hajiabadi–Langrehr–Wang (2026), *Generic-Group Barriers for Function-Hiding and Multi-Input Functional Encryption*, ePrint 2026/1149.

title: Fully tight lattice inner-product FE
subfield: Restricted FE, attribute-based encryption, and registration
open: Can we construct a lattice-based inner-product functional encryption scheme whose security reduction is fully tight? In other words, can the remaining reduction losses in known lattice IPFE constructions be eliminated while preserving compact ciphertexts and secret keys and the relevant adaptive security guarantees?
status: The current state of the art is the 2025 result of Han–Yi–Liu–Gu (*Tightly Secure Inner-Product Functional Encryption Revisited: Compact, Lattice-based, and More*, ePrint 2025/1613), which gives an almost-tight LWE-based construction — but not a fully tight one.
solved_when: A lattice IPFE scheme is given whose security reduction to LWE loses only a constant factor (fully tight, not merely almost-tight), while retaining compactness and the relevant adaptive security guarantees.
why: Tightness directly shrinks the parameters one must deploy, so schemes become practical for settings with many users and keys instead of suffering security degradation that grows with those quantities.
key_works: Han–Yi–Liu–Gu (2025), *Tightly Secure Inner-Product Functional Encryption Revisited: Compact, Lattice-based, and More*, ePrint 2025/1613.

title: Practical unbounded-dimension IPFE
subfield: Restricted FE, attribute-based encryption, and registration
open: Can unbounded-dimension inner-product functional encryption from lattices be implemented at a scale where the useful computation cost grows near-linearly, with an explicit treatment of output range, key issuance, and memory?
status: Unbounded IPFE from LWE has been constructed (Cini–Tairi (2026), *(Fine-Grained) Unbounded Inner-Product Functional Encryption from LWE*, ePrint 2026/062), so existence is settled; practical scalability is the open target.
solved_when: A working implementation of unbounded-dimension lattice IPFE achieves near-linear useful computation cost and documents its output range, key-issuance procedure, and memory behavior.
why: It would make encrypted analytics useful beyond short vectors.
key_works: Cini–Tairi (2026), *(Fine-Grained) Unbounded Inner-Product Functional Encryption from LWE*, ePrint 2026/062.

title: Public-key two-sided attribute-hiding predicate encryption
subfield: Restricted FE, attribute-based encryption, and registration
open: Can the new lattice-based two-sided attribute-hiding predicate-encryption scheme be lifted from the symmetric-key setting to the public-key setting? Formally, this asks for a public-key predicate-encryption scheme, from LWE-based techniques, that hides both the predicate and the attribute while retaining collusion resistance.

title: Polylogarithmic positional witness encryption
subfield: Witness encryption and conditional release
open: Can an indexed (positional) witness encryption scheme be built whose ciphertext overhead grows only polylogarithmically in the index bound N, without relying on full indistinguishability obfuscation? status: The 2026 construction (Nassar–Waters–Wu, *Obfuscating Non-Evasive Programs*, ePrint 2026/1932) extends witness encryption to non-evasive applications while retaining a restricted functionality boundary.

why: It measures how close witness encryption is to the full power of obfuscation; a positive answer would turn restricted primitives into the central object of iO, while a negative answer would expose a real complexity gap.

title: Safe public rerandomization of graded encodings
subfield: Multilinear maps and graded encodings
open: Can a graded encoding scheme support public rerandomization of encodings without leaking low-level zeroes or creating exploitable correlations across rerandomizations? Formally, is there a rerandomization procedure whose outputs are computationally independent of the computational history of the input encoding and reveal no information about low-level zeros?

solved_when: A candidate multilinear map construction admits a public rerandomization algorithm whose outputs provably expose no low-level zeros and admit no exploitable correlations across repeated rerandomizations.
why: Applications built on graded encodings need encodings that do not reveal their computational history; without such a procedure, rerandomization functionality that these applications require remains in dangerous tension with the security of candidate maps.
key_works: Garg–Gentry–Halevi (2013), ePrint 2012/610; Cheon et al. (2015), ePrint 2014/906.

solved_when: An explicit construction from algebraic geometry is given whose multilinear forms are efficiently representable and evaluable at higher multilinearity, with a plausible hardness argument for the resulting graded encoding.
why: A geometric foundation different from lattice and integer graded encodings could avoid entire classes of zeroizing attacks, opening a route to cryptographic multilinear maps that resists known cryptanalysis.

why: Applications built on multilinear maps need foundations that survive quantum algorithms.

title: Tight arity–noise–size tradeoffs
subfield: Multilinear maps and graded encodings
open: Are the steep, depth-dependent costs of existing multilinear map candidates forced by the mathematics, or just by our constructions? status: Existing candidate constructions, such as Garg–Gentry–Halevi (2013), *Candidate Multilinear Maps from Ideal Lattices*, ePrint 2012/610, exhibit substantial depth-dependent costs, but no complete matching lower-bound theory is known.
solved_when: Matching upper and lower bounds relating multiplicative arity, noise growth, encoding size, and correctness are established, so that the depth-dependent costs achieved by known candidates are provably optimal up to constants.
why: It would separate unavoidable costs of high-arity computation from artifacts of current constructions, telling cryptographers whether to search for fundamentally better graded encodings or stop looking.

why: It would deliver rich programmable PRF capabilities without relying on general-purpose obfuscation, which remains without standard-assumption foundations.

title: CPRFs for arbitrary purified predicates

open: Can lattice-based constrained pseudorandom functions be extended to any efficiently computable family of predicates whose authorized sets are pairwise disjoint? Formally, construct CPRFs from LWE-type assumptions for arbitrary such "purified" predicate families.

solved_when: A CPRF construction (with a proof of pseudorandomness on unconstrained inputs and constraint security) is given, based on lattice/LWE assumptions, for every efficiently computable predicate family whose authorized sets are pairwise disjoint.
why: Disjointness of authorized sets may permit a level of expressiveness that is provably unavailable for unrestricted, overlapping constraint families.

title: Constraint-private predicated-range CPRFs
subfield: Constrained pseudorandom functions
open: Can the constraints in the lattice-based predicated-range constrained PRF be hidden from the users who receive constrained keys? Formally, is there a constraint-private variant of the construction that conceals the predicate defining the constrained range while preserving its existing collusion-resistance guarantees?
status: Range-constraint privacy remains explicitly open; the underlying collusion-resistant predicated-range CPRF from LWE is due to Cheng–Goyal (2026), *Collusion-Resistant Constrained PRFs for Compute-&-Compare Predicates from LWE*, ePrint 2026/1874. why: The intervals and predicates that define access rights can themselves be sensitive — for example, range queries may leak which records or attributes a querier is permitted to touch — so without constraint privacy the delegating party's policy is exposed.

title: General one-key private CPRFs from OWFs

why: It would isolate a useful private-program capability — delegating constrained evaluations without revealing the constrained function — at a strictly weaker assumption than public-key cryptography.
key_works: Bi–Ma–Dai (2026), *Limits on the Power of Private Constrained PRFs*, DOI: 10.4230/LIPIcs.ITC.2026.2.

status: Recent work by Bi–Ma–Dai (2026), *Limits on the Power of Private Constrained PRFs* (DOI: 10.4230/LIPIcs.ITC.2026.2), excludes specified black-box constructions but does not rule out unrestricted, non-black-box implications.

why: A resolution in either direction would place private CPRFs precisely in the assumption hierarchy, clarifying whether they live in Minicrypt or already reach Cryptomania.

title: Private adaptive delegation of constraints
subfield: Constrained pseudorandom functions
open: Can constrained-key holders in a constrained PRF securely derive stricter constrained keys of their own, so that neither the parent nor the child predicate is revealed and adaptive collusion among key holders learns nothing beyond their individual constraints?

solved_when: A constrained PRF construction is given in which a key for predicate $f$ can derive a key for any stricter predicate $f'$, with predicate privacy for both parent and child keys and provable collusion resistance against adaptive key requests.
why: It would enable hierarchical delegation of capabilities inside an organization without leaking the policy structure governing who holds which constraints.

title: Tight constrained-key size lower bounds
subfield: Constrained pseudorandom functions
open: For constrained pseudorandom functions, can we characterize exactly how large a constrained key must be, as a function of the predicate complexity, the permitted leakage, and the collusion count? A tight answer would give matching upper and lower bounds on key size across this parameter space.
status: Existing family-specific constructions and separations do not give a complete quantitative classification; see Langrehr (2025/2026), ePrint 2025/1338, and Davidson et al. (2018/2020), ePrint 2018/982.
solved_when: For each setting of predicate complexity, permitted leakage, and collusion count, there exist matching constructions and lower bounds on constrained-key size as a function of these parameters.
why: A tight characterization would separate the unavoidable cost of describing a constrained capability from key-size overhead that is merely an artifact of inefficient constructions.
key_works: Langrehr (2025/2026), ePrint 2025/1338; Davidson et al. (2018/2020), ePrint 2018/982.

title: Optimal post-quantum threshold tracing without a ramp
subfield: Traitor tracing and accountable broadcast
open: Can threshold traitor tracing achieve the optimal dependence on the number of users without giving up post-quantum security? Formally, is there a scheme with polylogarithmic user-count dependence, ordinary (non-ramp) thresholds, and security from plain LWE?
status: The schemes achieving optimal classical parameters rely on pairings; the known lattice candidate requires special secret sharing and ramp thresholds. (Das–Datta–Partap–Sasmal–Zhandry (2025/2026), *Optimal Threshold Traitor Tracing*, ePrint 2025/2154.)
solved_when: A threshold traitor-tracing scheme is constructed that is post-quantum secure under plain LWE, supports ordinary thresholds (no ramp structure and no special secret sharing), and achieves polylogarithmic dependence on the number of users.
why: It would merge compact accountability with post-quantum security, removing the gap between the pairing-based schemes with optimal classical parameters and the current lattice candidates.
key_works: Das–Datta–Partap–Sasmal–Zhandry (2025/2026), *Optimal Threshold Traitor Tracing*, ePrint 2025/2154.

title: The secret-sharing ingredient for lattice threshold tracing
subfield: Traitor tracing and accountable broadcast
open: Can we explicitly construct the special secret-sharing schemes that the optimal lattice threshold-tracing candidate needs, with the required parameters? These schemes are a distinct unresolved dependency of the tracing construction, not a restatement of the tracing problem itself.
status: This remains a separate unresolved dependency rather than another statement of the entire tracing problem; the underlying tracing candidate appears in Das et al. (2025/2026), *Optimal Threshold Traitor Tracing*, ePrint 2025/2154. Related lines of inquiry include linear secret-sharing complexity and monotone span programs.
solved_when: An explicit construction of the required secret-sharing schemes is given, meeting the parameters needed by the optimal lattice threshold-tracing candidate.
why: A solution would complete a concrete candidate construction for optimal lattice threshold tracing.
key_works: Das et al. (2025/2026), *Optimal Threshold Traitor Tracing*, ePrint 2025/2154.

title: Closing the many-traitor tracing gap
subfield: Traitor tracing and accountable broadcast
open: When a coalition of traitors colludes to build a pirate decoder, can we trace back all (or most) of them, and what are the fundamental limits? In particular, do the known linear-type lower bounds on the tracing overhead match what is achievable, or are the quadratic-type constructions for recovering a full threshold-sized coalition far from optimal?
status: The 2026 lower bounds of Boneh–Partap–Zhandry (*Catching Many Traitors in Threshold Traitor Tracing: Lower Bounds and Constructions*, ePrint 2026/1523) carry model qualifications and do not settle the full optimum. Related techniques include adaptive group testing and list recovery.
solved_when: Matching upper and lower bounds are established for recovering many — specifically threshold-sized — coalition members, closing the gap between the linear-type lower bounds and the quadratic-type constructions.
why: Identifying a single participant may not restore system security; a solution tells us the true cost of full accountability in traitor-tracing schemes.
key_works: Boneh–Partap–Zhandry (2026), *Catching Many Traitors in Threshold Traitor Tracing: Lower Bounds and Constructions*, ePrint 2026/1523.

title: Many-traitor tracing from polynomial hardness
subfield: Traitor tracing and accountable broadcast
open: Can strong recovery guarantees against many colluding traitors be achieved from polynomial hardness assumptions alone, without relying on exponential hardness in any part of the construction?
status: The 2026 construction of Boneh–Partap–Zhandry (*Catching Many Traitors in Threshold Traitor Tracing*, ePrint 2026/1523) achieves the many-traitor setting, but its hardness scaling — specifically the exponential-hardness requirement — remains a substantive qualification.
solved_when: A traitor-tracing scheme is constructed that retains the many-traitor recovery guarantees of the 2026 construction while requiring only polynomial hardness assumptions, eliminating the exponential hardness scaling entirely.
why: It would improve the credibility and efficiency of concrete parameter choices for traitor tracing deployments.
key_works: Boneh–Partap–Zhandry (2026), *Catching Many Traitors in Threshold Traitor Tracing*, ePrint 2026/1523.

title: Post-quantum decentralized multi-authority tracing
subfield: Traitor tracing and accountable broadcast
open: Can expressive decentralized traitor tracing be built from ordinary post-quantum assumptions — lattices, codes, or hashes — rather than from group-based foundations, while keeping parameters compact? In other words, is there a construction matching the functionality of the current group-based scheme whose security reduces to standard post-quantum assumptions without asymptotic blow-up in keys, ciphertexts, or tracing material?
status: The current state of the art is the 2026 construction of Datta–Schädlich–Tairi (ePrint 2026/1268), which achieves expressive decentralized tracing but relies on MDDH-style group assumptions; no post-quantum replacement is known.
solved_when: A construction is given for decentralized multi-authority tracing with the expressiveness of the group-based scheme, proved secure under ordinary post-quantum assumptions (no MDDH-style group assumptions), with parameters compact — no asymptotic degradation relative to the 2026 group-based baseline.
why: Accountability infrastructure should not fail when discrete-log assumptions fail; a quantum adversary breaking the group foundation would silently destroy traceability across the whole decentralized broadcast system.
key_works: Datta–Schädlich–Tairi (2026), ePrint 2026/1268.

title: Public tracing without a substantial parameter penalty
subfield: Traitor tracing and accountable broadcast
open: Can a decentralized traitor-tracing scheme allow anyone to publicly run the tracing procedure and verify its soundness, while matching the efficiency of the best privately traceable schemes?
status: Public-traceability variants of decentralized traitor tracing exist but impose additional costs (Datta–Schädlich–Tairi (2026), *Decentralized Multi-Authority (Attribute-Based) Traitor Tracing*, ePrint 2026/1268); no scheme currently matches private-tracing efficiency with public traceability.
solved_when: A publicly traceable decentralized traitor-tracing scheme is constructed whose parameters (key/ciphertext sizes and tracing overhead) match those of the state-of-the-art privately traceable decentralized schemes, up to at most a constant factor, with sound public tracing.
why: Public accountability should not require a privileged tracing authority or substantially larger artifacts; closing the gap removes the main excuse for centralized tracing in accountable broadcast systems.
key_works: Datta–Schädlich–Tairi (2026), *Decentralized Multi-Authority (Attribute-Based) Traitor Tracing*, ePrint 2026/1268.

bib.title: Public tracing without a substantial parameter penalty

title: Tracing stateful quantum pirate decoders
subfield: Traitor tracing and accountable broadcast
open: Can a broadcast authority trace a pirate decoder whose users may hold and reprogram arbitrary quantum state, rather than a resettable classical device? A satisfactory answer would give a tracing procedure with explicit success and false-accusation bounds for such stateful quantum adversaries.
status: Stronger classical insider models do not automatically handle destructive quantum queries; the problem remains open. Related to Bormet–Othman (2026), *Threshold Traitor Tracing with Partial-Insider Resilience*, ePrint 2026/1059, and to work on quantum process learning and gentle measurement.
solved_when: A tracing scheme is constructed and proved sound against stateful quantum pirate decoders, with explicit quantitative bounds on tracing success probability and false-accusation probability.
why: Once the pirate can carry quantum state, the order of tracing queries and the disturbance they cause to that state become security-relevant, so existing tracing guarantees no longer carry over.
key_works: Bormet–Othman (2026), *Threshold Traitor Tracing with Partial-Insider Resilience*, ePrint 2026/1059.

title: Expressive multi-sender traceable FE
subfield: Traitor tracing and accountable broadcast
open: Can we build traceable multi-client functional encryption supporting quadratic or general circuit functionalities, rather than just inner products, while still retaining meaningful tracing guarantees?
status: The 2025 multi-sender construction (Do–Mac–Nguyen–Phan–Vu, *Traitor Tracing in Multi-sender Setting*, ePrint 2025/364) establishes an inner-product baseline; nothing beyond inner products is currently known.
solved_when: A lattice-based multi-sender traceable functional encryption scheme is constructed for quadratic or general circuit functionality with meaningful tracing guarantees preserved.
why: It would bring accountability — the ability to identify misbehaving senders — to richer collaborative encrypted analytics beyond simple linear computations.
key_works: Do–Mac–Nguyen–Phan–Vu (2025), *Traitor Tracing in Multi-sender Setting*, ePrint 2025/364.

title: Succinct publicly checkable non-framing evidence
subfield: Traitor tracing and accountable broadcast
open: Can a traitor-tracing system produce short, publicly verifiable evidence that a given accusation against a user is correct, so that the accusation neither leaks honest users' keys nor can be fabricated by a malicious tracer to frame an innocent user?
status: Currently, an algorithm that privately returns an identity is known to be weaker than this evidentiary functionality, which remains unrealized. Related directions include zero-knowledge attribution and accountable fault diagnosis; see Bormet–Othman (2026), *Threshold Traitor Tracing with Partial-Insider Resilience*, ePrint 2026/1059.
solved_when: A construction exists in which tracing output is a compact, publicly checkable proof of accusation correctness, with privacy for honest keys and non-framing against malicious tracers; this strictly improves on algorithms that merely return an identity privately.
why: Without it, a cryptographic accusation is just an unverifiable claim by the tracer; with it, tracing gains the independently checkable support needed for accountability in broadcast systems.
key_works: Bormet–Othman (2026), *Threshold Traitor Tracing with Partial-Insider Resilience*, ePrint 2026/1059.

title: Point-function copy protection from plain LWE
subfield: Copy protection and secure software leasing
open: Can suitable unpredictable point-function distributions be copy-protected assuming only the plain Learning With Errors (LWE) assumption, avoiding post-quantum indistinguishability obfuscation? In other words, can copy protection for this foundational class be based directly on standard lattice assumptions?
status: Stronger correlated-challenge copy protection has now been constructed under stronger assumptions, so bare existence of such protections is no longer the open question; the remaining gap is basing plain point-function copy protection on ordinary LWE. Key work: Behera–Çakan–Goyal (2026), *Decisional Monogamy-of-Entanglement for Coset States and Applications to Unclonable Cryptography with Correlated Challenges*, arXiv:2608.18841.
solved_when: A construction of copy protection for suitable unpredictable point-function distributions is given whose security reduces to plain LWE, with no post-quantum iO or stronger correlated-challenge assumptions in the reduction.
why: Point functions are the foundational test case for copy protection; a plain-LWE construction would sharply reduce the assumptions needed for unclonable cryptography and likely unlock copy protection for broader function classes.
key_works: Behera–Çakan–Goyal (2026), *Decisional Monogamy-of-Entanglement for Coset States and Applications to Unclonable Cryptography with Correlated Challenges*, arXiv:2608.18841.

bib.title: Point-function copy protection from plain LWE

title: Reusable PRF copy protection without iO
subfield: Copy protection and secure software leasing
open: Can a cryptographically useful family of PRFs be copy-protected from ordinary post-quantum assumptions, without resorting to indistinguishability obfuscation — and, in particular, without falling back on the weaker leasing model that requires the key to be returned?
status: Copy protection and secure key leasing have different adversarial success conditions; the current record cites only key-leasing-style results for PRFs, with return requirements, rather than full copy protection. Key works: Liu–Liu–Qian–Zhandry (2022), *Collusion Resistant Copy-Protection for Watermarkable Functionalities*; Kitagawa–Nishimaki–Pappu (2025/2026), arXiv:2510.04754.
solved_when: A copy-protection scheme (not merely secure key leasing) for a useful PRF family is constructed and proved secure against the standard copy-protection adversary, from post-quantum assumptions weaker than iO.
why: PRFs are a canonical building block, so copy-protecting them would unlock many reusable protected functionalities beyond the specific primitives currently known.
key_works: Liu–Liu–Qian–Zhandry (2022), *Collusion Resistant Copy-Protection for Watermarkable Functionalities*; Kitagawa–Nishimaki–Pappu (2025/2026), arXiv:2510.04754.

title: Sharp distributional requirements for copy protection
subfield: Copy protection and secure software leasing
open: Which distributions of functions admit copy protection and secure software leasing? In particular, what are the exact unpredictability or entropy conditions under which point functions and compute-and-compare functions can be copy-protected, and do matching attacks rule out protection for every distribution failing those conditions?
status: Recent positive results, imposing meaningful distributional restrictions, are due to Behera–Çakan–Goyal (2026), arXiv:2608.18841. Related directions include min-entropy extraction and distribution-dependent learning.
solved_when: A characterization is proved: copy protection (or secure software leasing) succeeds for point functions and compute-and-compare functions exactly when the input distribution meets the stated entropy or unpredictability condition, with attacks showing protection fails below that threshold.
why: Real protected programs are not sampled uniformly, so positive results that hold only for uniform distributions leave the practically relevant cases unresolved; sharp distributional conditions tell us exactly when protecting deployed software is possible.
key_works: Behera–Çakan–Goyal (2026), arXiv:2608.18841.

bib.title: Sharp distributional requirements for copy protection

title: Optimal protected-state size under collusion
subfield: Copy protection and secure software leasing
open: How much quantum memory must a copy-protected program necessarily occupy when security must hold against \(k\) colluding users who jointly try to create \(k+1\) usable copies? Formally, the question is to match the known upper bounds with matching lower bounds on the required quantum-state size for \(k\)-to-\(k+1\) copy-protection security as \(k\) grows.
status: Collusion-resistant copy-protection constructions exist — see Liu–Liu–Qian–Zhandry (2022), *Collusion Resistant Copy-Protection for Watermarkable Functionalities* — but the optimal dependence of the protected-state size on the collusion parameter \(k\) remains open as a separate quantitative frontier. Related tools include quantum random-access codes and copy-complexity lower bounds.
solved_when: Upper and lower bounds on the protected-state size for \(k\)-to-\(k+1\) copy-protection security agree (up to constants) for all \(k\), pinning down the optimal dependence on \(k\).
why: Without tight bounds, a legitimate licensee could be forced to allocate an enormous quantum memory to run a protected program; tight bounds guarantee licenses stay as small as security permits.
key_works: Liu–Liu–Qian–Zhandry (2022), *Collusion Resistant Copy-Protection for Watermarkable Functionalities*.

title: Noise-tolerant reusable copy protection
subfield: Copy protection and secure software leasing
open: Can copy-protected or securely leased programs remain both correct and copy-protected when the underlying storage suffers explicit noise and the gates are imperfect? A satisfactory answer should establish security with a nonzero physical-noise threshold.
status: Existing constructions are stated for ideal, noiseless settings, and ideal-state constructions do not automatically provide fault-tolerant security. Behera–Çakan–Goyal (2026), arXiv:2608.18841, represent the current ideal-state state of the art.
solved_when: A construction exists that retains correctness and anti-copying security under an explicit storage-noise model and imperfect gates, provably tolerating noise up to some strictly positive threshold.
why: Without noise tolerance, copy-protected quantum software breaks on real hardware; a fault-tolerant construction would bridge idealized copy protection and deployable secure software leasing.
key_works: Behera–Çakan–Goyal (2026), arXiv:2608.18841.

title: Side-channel-secure copy protection
subfield: Copy protection and secure software leasing
open: Can we build a copy-protection or secure software leasing scheme whose classical operations — the preparation of the protected state, its evaluation, error correction, and final disposal — leak nothing that compromises security? More precisely: a construction in which the classical side-channel behavior across the entire life cycle of the protected program is accounted for, rather than only the idealized cryptographic interface.
status: Existing secure software leasing schemes (Ananth–La Placa, 2020/2021, *Secure Software Leasing*, arXiv:2005.05289) do not account for classical leakage during the protected program's life cycle; the observation motivating this problem is that no-cloning does not prevent a classical implementation from exposing the protected function.
solved_when: A construction of secure software leasing (in the style of Ananth–La Placa) is given with a formal treatment of classical leakage arising during protected-state preparation, evaluation, error correction, and disposal, together with a security proof covering those phases.
why: Physical protection of the protected function is ineffective if an ordinary log file or timing channel observable during normal use reveals the secret; no-cloning alone does not stop a classical implementation from exposing the protected function.
key_works: Ananth–La Placa (2020/2021), *Secure Software Leasing*, arXiv:2005.05289.

title: Domain-samplable trapdoor-function leasing from plain LWE
subfield: Copy protection and secure software leasing
open: Can trapdoor functions with secure key leasing — where the lease can be revoked, deleting the user's ability to evaluate — be constructed from plain LWE while still supporting an efficient public algorithm for sampling valid function inputs? A satisfactory solution should, more formally, achieve the strongest relevant collusion resistance alongside the domain-sampling property.
status: The 2026 work of Kitagawa–Nishimaki–Shirakawa–Yamakawa (*Trapdoor Functions with Secure Key Leasing and Copy Protection*, ePrint 2026/1913) distinguishes constructions with and without domain samplers, and shows the assumptions involved are not interchangeable.
solved_when: A construction of leased trapdoor functions from plain LWE is given whose security holds against the strongest relevant collusion guarantee and whose domain can be sampled efficiently without any secret information, with a proof of both leasing security and input-sampling correctness.
why: In most applications users must be able to generate valid inputs to the trapdoor function on their own; a leasing scheme without a public domain sampler does not support this, so it fails to replace unleased trapdoor functions in practice.
key_works: Kitagawa–Nishimaki–Shirakawa–Yamakawa (2026), *Trapdoor Functions with Secure Key Leasing and Copy Protection*, ePrint 2026/1913.

bib.title: Domain-samplable trapdoor-function leasing from plain LWE

title: Low-cost publicly verifiable leasing
subfield: Copy protection and secure software leasing
open: Can secure software leasing be realized so that anyone — not a trusted or resource-heavy party — can check that a leased program has been returned and rendered useless, while the scheme still tolerates adaptive verification queries, collusion among lessees, and near-linear client processing with compact certificates?
status: Public verification and verification-query resilience have each advanced; the complete efficiency combination must be demonstrated. Key work: Kitagawa–Nishimaki–Pappu (2025/2026), *Collusion-Resistant Quantum Secure Key Leasing Beyond Decryption*, arXiv:2510.04754.
solved_when: A leasing scheme is constructed that simultaneously achieves public return verification, adaptive verification-query resilience, collusion resistance, and near-linear client processing cost with compact certificates, and the complete efficiency combination is demonstrated.
why: It removes the need for an expensive or privileged return verifier, making leasing practical as a deployable primitive rather than a theoretical ideal.
key_works: Kitagawa–Nishimaki–Pappu (2025/2026), *Collusion-Resistant Quantum Secure Key Leasing Beyond Decryption*, arXiv:2510.04754.

title: Leasing secure against malicious lessors
subfield: Copy protection and secure software leasing
open: Can secure software leasing be made two-sided, so that a lessee is protected against a malicious lessor — one who may run a corrupted key-generation procedure, induce selective failures, or link a lessee's behavior across sessions — without giving up the lessor's anti-piracy guarantees? In other words, is there a leasing scheme whose security proof holds for both parties simultaneously against malicious counterparts?
status: Existing leasing notions guarantee security only for the lessor, leaving two-sided security as a separate open problem; the key recent work in this direction is Kitagawa–Nishimaki–Pappu (2025/2026), arXiv:2510.04754, and the problem connects to malicious-device security and selective-failure leakage.
solved_when: A leasing scheme (and proof) exists that simultaneously preserves the standard anti-piracy / uncloneability guarantees for the honest lessor and protects the lessee against malicious key generation, selective-failure attacks, and cross-session linking by the lessor.
why: Without lessee-side security, quantum licensing risks creating a privileged surveillance and sabotage interface controlled by the lessor; a two-sided guarantee is needed so that protection against piracy does not come at the cost of the user's security.
key_works: Kitagawa–Nishimaki–Pappu (2025/2026), arXiv:2510.04754.

title: Optimal rate of statistical uncloneable encryption
subfield: Uncloneable encryption, quantum money, and one-shot capabilities
open: What is the maximum rate at which uncloneable encryption can transmit classical messages per qubit sent? That is, determine the best message-to-qubit rate compatible with efficient encryption, negligible cloning advantage, and explicit key cost.
status: A 2026 preprint by Bhattacharyya–Broadbent–Culf (*Statistically Secure Uncloneable Encryption of Arbitrary Messages*, arXiv:2607.28561) constructs statistically secure one-time encryption of arbitrary-length messages, but achieving the optimal rate remains stronger than what is known.
solved_when: A scheme (or a matching lower and upper bound) is given whose message-to-qubit rate is shown optimal among schemes achieving negligible cloning advantage with efficient encryption and explicitly quantified key cost.
why: It answers how much quantum communication unclonability fundamentally costs, pinning down the overhead that any statistically secure uncloneable-encryption scheme must pay.
key_works: Bhattacharyya–Broadbent–Culf (2026), *Statistically Secure Uncloneable Encryption of Arbitrary Messages*, arXiv:2607.28561.

title: Optimal key cost for many-message statistical uncloneability
subfield: Uncloneable encryption, quantum money, and one-shot capabilities
open: Does statistical uncloneability of encrypted messages persist — at what key cost — when a single key protects many ciphertexts rather than one? A full answer should characterize how key material amortizes or recycles across many messages, together with matching lower bounds against adversaries attacking all ciphertexts jointly.
status: One-time arbitrary-message security does not settle the many-message resource frontier; the amortization regime remains uncharacterized. Key works: Bhattacharyya–Broadbent–Culf (2026), arXiv:2607.28561.
solved_when: A characterization of secure key amortization and recycling across many ciphertexts is given, with upper bounds matched by lower bounds against joint attacks on all ciphertexts.
why: It would distinguish genuinely reusable protection from merely repeating one-time provisioning, settling the many-message resource frontier that one-time security leaves open.
key_works: Bhattacharyya–Broadbent–Culf (2026), arXiv:2607.28561.

title: Loss-tolerant uncloneable encryption
subfield: Uncloneable encryption, quantum money, and one-shot capabilities
open: Can uncloneable encryption be made to survive realistic channel loss, so that an adversary who loses some of the transmitted quantum states still cannot extract usable clones of the key or message?
status: Existing theorems on uncloneable encryption, including statistically secure schemes for arbitrary messages (Bhattacharyya–Broadbent–Culf, 2026, arXiv:2607.28561), are proved for noiseless transmission and do not establish unclonability under erasures or photon loss.
solved_when: A construction of uncloneable encryption is given whose security guarantee degrades gracefully under erasures and photon loss, with a proof that adversarial postselection over lost messages cannot amplify the adversary's success probability.
why: Loss is unavoidable in quantum communication, so without loss tolerance the known unclonability guarantees do not translate into a physical guarantee for any realistic deployment.
key_works: Bhattacharyya–Broadbent–Culf (2026), *Statistically Secure Uncloneable Encryption of Arbitrary Messages*, arXiv:2607.28561.

title: Optimal overhead of multi-copy security amplification
subfield: Uncloneable encryption, quantum money, and one-shot capabilities
open: When a cryptographic scheme secure against a single adversary is upgraded to remain secure against colluding holders of many copies, how much must the state size, computation time, and security parameter grow? The goal is to improve, or prove optimal, the overhead of generic compilers that transform collusion resistance into full multi-copy security.
status: A generic upgrade from collusion resistance to multi-copy security already exists (Çakan–Goyal–Kitagawa–Nishimaki–Yamakawa (2025), *Multi-Copy Security in Unclonable Cryptography*, ePrint 2025/1921); the open target is its quantitative efficiency.
solved_when: The quantitative losses in state size, computation, and security of the multi-copy compiler are either reduced beyond the current bounds or matched by a proof that no generic compiler can do better.
why: Excessive overhead means that protecting schemes against multi-copy attacks multiplies quantum resource requirements unnecessarily, making the upgraded schemes impractical; tight bounds tell us when this cost is inherent.
key_works: Çakan–Goyal–Kitagawa–Nishimaki–Yamakawa (2025), *Multi-Copy Security in Unclonable Cryptography*, ePrint 2025/1921.

bib.title: Optimal overhead of multi-copy security amplification

title: Physical certified deletion with complete side-channel accounting
subfield: Uncloneable encryption, quantum money, and one-shot capabilities
open: Can we build a physical implementation of certified deletion in which the security analysis accounts for the full behavior of the actual apparatus — preparation errors, detector imperfections, classical logs, and residual storage? Formally, the goal is a demonstration whose security model provably covers these side channels rather than an abstract certificate over idealized devices.
status: Abstract deletion certificates do not certify an unmodeled physical device. Related directions include device-independent security and data-remanence measurement; see Chen–Ji–Luo (2026), *Linearly Homomorphic Secret Sharing and Multi-Party Computation with Unanimously Verifiable Deletion*, ePrint 2026/1673.
solved_when: A certified-deletion demonstration is achieved whose security model includes preparation errors, detector behavior, classical logs, and residual storage.
why: It would connect mathematical deletion guarantees to actual data custody, so that a deletion certificate certifies the physical device rather than an unmodeled abstraction.
key_works: Chen–Ji–Luo (2026), *Linearly Homomorphic Secret Sharing and Multi-Party Computation with Unanimously Verifiable Deletion*, ePrint 2026/1673.

title: Fault-tolerant public quantum-money lifecycles
subfield: Uncloneable encryption, quantum money, and one-shot capabilities
open: Can a public quantum-money scheme be operated as a working banknote — repeatedly verified, transferred, and stored by honest users — while tolerating quantified noise and correcting errors in a way that does not open the door to counterfeiting?
status: Existing quantum-money constructions are established asymptotically, but no physical lifecycle demonstration of repeated use with quantified noise tolerance and security-preserving error correction exists. Key reference: Doliskani (2025/2026), *Public-Key Quantum Money From Standard Assumptions (In The Generic Model)*, ePrint 2025/092.
solved_when: A physical-lifecycle demonstration exists in which a public quantum banknote undergoes repeated public verification, transfer, and storage, with explicit quantitative bounds on tolerated noise and error-correction steps that provably preserve the scheme's security.
why: A banknote must survive legitimate use as well as counterfeiting attempts; without fault tolerance under honest handling, asymptotic money constructions cannot be deployed as actual currency.
key_works: Doliskani (2025/2026), *Public-Key Quantum Money From Standard Assumptions (In The Generic Model)*, ePrint 2025/092.

title: Genuinely refresh-free unrestricted FHE
subfield: Fully homomorphic encryption: construction foundations
open: Can fully homomorphic encryption support arbitrary polynomial-depth computation with fixed parameters, while avoiding any mechanism that refreshes ciphertexts — including bootstrapping, encrypted-secret-key refresh material, or any substituted operation playing the refresh role? Formally: fixed-parameter FHE for unbounded polynomial depth with no homomorphic decryption step and no functional equivalent thereof.
status: Leved "without bootstrapping" results (e.g., Brakerski–Gentry–Vaikuntanathan, ePrint 2011/277) require a preset depth bound and thus do not meet this specification; the recent construction from lattice isomorphism (Branco–Malavolta–Maradni, *Fully-Homomorphic Encryption from Lattice Isomorphism*, ePrint 2025/993) likewise does not satisfy it.
solved_when: A construction is given that supports arbitrary polynomial-depth homomorphic evaluation with fixed parameters (no per-depth parameter growth) and provably uses no bootstrapping, no encrypted-secret-key refresh material, and no substituted operation serving the same refresh role.
why: It would eliminate the recurring maintenance operation from encrypted computation, removing the dominant recurring cost and design constraint in current FHE schemes.
key_works: Brakerski–Gentry–Vaikuntanathan, ePrint 2011/277; Branco–Malavolta–Maradni (2025), *Fully-Homomorphic Encryption from Lattice Isomorphism*, ePrint 2025/993.

title: Coding-based general FHE
subfield: Fully homomorphic encryption: construction foundations
open: Can fully homomorphic encryption for general circuits be built from a conventional code-based hardness assumption, rather than from lattices or assumptions isomorphic to them? In other words, is there a compact, general-purpose FHE scheme whose security rests on average-case decoding or related coding-theoretic problems?
status: The state of the art diversifies lattice foundations only: lattice-isomorphism constructions (Branco–Malavolta–Maradni (2025), *Fully-Homomorphic Encryption from Lattice Isomorphism*, ePrint 2025/993) are not code-based FHE, and no code-based general FHE is known.
solved_when: A compact general FHE scheme exists whose security reduces to a conventional code-based hardness assumption, with no reliance on lattice or lattice-isomorphism assumptions.
why: It would supply substantial post-quantum assumption diversity, giving FHE an security foundation independent of lattices.
key_works: Branco–Malavolta–Maradni (2025), *Fully-Homomorphic Encryption from Lattice Isomorphism*, ePrint 2025/993.

title: Removing circularity from lattice-isomorphism FHE
subfield: Fully homomorphic encryption: construction foundations
open: Can fully homomorphic encryption supporting arbitrary-depth evaluation be built from a standard lattice-isomorphism assumption alone, without assuming circular security? Formally, construct an unrestricted-depth (non-leveled) FHE scheme whose security reduces to a lattice-isomorphism problem, with no additional circular-security hypothesis.
status: Recent work supplies FHE from lattice isomorphism under an added circular-security assumption, and separate leveled constructions without it; unrestricted-depth FHE from the assumption alone remains open. (Branco–Malavolta–Maradni, 2025, ePrint 2025/993; Bennett–Lai–Stephens-Davidowitz, 2026, *Advanced Cryptography from Lattice Isomorphism—New Constructions of IBE and FHE*, ePrint 2026/465.)
solved_when: An unrestricted-depth FHE scheme is given with a proof of security reducing solely to a lattice-isomorphism assumption, with no circular-security assumption invoked anywhere in the argument.
why: It would remove the extra trust assumption currently needed for this new foundation for homomorphic encryption, making lattice isomorphism a cleaner standalone basis for FHE.
key_works: Branco–Malavolta–Maradni (2025), ePrint 2025/993; Bennett–Lai–Stephens-Davidowitz (2026), *Advanced Cryptography from Lattice Isomorphism—New Constructions of IBE and FHE*, ePrint 2026/465.

title: FHE from arbitrary public-key encryption
subfield: Fully homomorphic encryption: construction foundations
open: Can fully homomorphic encryption be built from any public-key encryption scheme, if we allow fully non-black-box constructions? Formally, does compact FHE follow from the mere existence of PKE with no additional structural assumptions?
status: No such derivation is known; existing constructions use substantially more structure than arbitrary public-key encryption (e.g., Brakerski–Gentry–Vaikuntanathan, ePrint 2011/277). Related lines of attack include cryptographic completeness and non-black-box separations, as in Bennett–Lai–Stephens-Davidowitz (2026), ePrint 2026/465.
solved_when: A construction of compact FHE is exhibited whose only assumption is the existence of public-key encryption, with unrestricted use of non-black-box techniques; alternatively, a separation ruling out such a derivation.
why: It determines whether homomorphic computation is a genuinely additional cryptographic foundation or merely a consequence of encryption itself — a basic question about what the abstract notion of secrecy already buys us.
key_works: Brakerski–Gentry–Vaikuntanathan, ePrint 2011/277; Bennett–Lai–Stephens-Davidowitz (2026), ePrint 2026/465.

title: Multi-hop CCA-compatible FHE
subfield: Fully homomorphic encryption: construction foundations
open: Can fully homomorphic encryption simultaneously support chosen-ciphertext-compatible security and multiple rounds of homomorphic evaluation, under assumptions and ciphertext compactness comparable to existing constructions? In other words, can useful CCA guarantees be extended beyond a single evaluation hop?
status: The recent standard-model construction of Yang–Yu–Susilo (*Fully Homomorphic Encryption with Chosen-Ciphertext Security from LWE*, ePrint 2026/1756, 2025/2026) is one-hop and uses circular-secure LWE; ordinary unrestricted CCA2 is known to be incompatible with public malleability, so the guarantee must be of a restricted, chosen-ciphertext-compatible form.
solved_when: A construction achieves FHE that is CCA-compatible while supporting repeated (multi-hop) homomorphic evaluation, with security resting on assumptions no stronger than circular-secure LWE and ciphertexts remaining compact.
why: Encrypted results in realistic deployments often pass through multiple independent evaluators; a one-hop guarantee forces re-encryption or trust at every intermediate step.
key_works: Yang–Yu–Susilo (2025/2026), *Fully Homomorphic Encryption with Chosen-Ciphertext Security from LWE*, ePrint 2026/1756.

title: Near-baseline malicious circuit privacy
subfield: Fully homomorphic encryption: construction foundations
open: Can fully homomorphic encryption achieve circuit privacy against malicious adversaries — where even a maliciously generated ciphertext leaks nothing about the circuit being evaluated — with only a small constant-factor blow-up in ciphertext size and evaluation cost over the non-private baseline?
status: Maliciously circuit-private FHE already exists, including black-box transformations (Döttling–Dujmovic, 2022, *Maliciously Circuit-Private FHE from Information-Theoretic Principles*, ePrint 2022/495); achieving low concrete overhead remains the open target.
solved_when: A maliciously circuit-private FHE scheme (or black-box transformation) is given whose ciphertext-size and evaluation-cost overhead over the underlying scheme is bounded by a small constant factor.
why: The evaluated program may contain sensitive models or policies, so circuit privacy is what keeps them hidden even from the key holder or a malicious evaluator.
key_works: Döttling–Dujmovic (2022), *Maliciously Circuit-Private FHE from Information-Theoretic Principles*, ePrint 2022/495.

title: Fully succinct unleveled multi-key FHE from plain LWE
subfield: Fully homomorphic encryption: construction foundations
open: Can we build a multi-key fully homomorphic encryption scheme that is fully succinct — with keys and ciphertexts independent of the number of participants — while also supporting unlimited computation depth, all under the plain LWE assumption?
status: The 2026 fully succinct result (Afshar–Goyal, *Fully-Succinct Multi-Key FHE & Rate-1 Simulatable Threshold Decryption from LWE*, ePrint 2026/1683) achieves full succinctness but is leveled; participant independence does not remove that leveled qualification.
solved_when: A construction exists that simultaneously achieves participant-count-independent keys and ciphertexts, unrestricted (unleveled) homomorphic depth, and full succinctness, proven secure under ordinary LWE.
why: It would unify the two major compactness goals of multi-key FHE — participant independence and depth independence — in a single construction, which current approaches achieve only separately.
key_works: Afshar–Goyal (2026), *Fully-Succinct Multi-Key FHE & Rate-1 Simulatable Threshold Decryption from LWE*, ePrint 2026/1683.

title: Efficient membership changes in fast multi-key FHE
subfield: Fully homomorphic encryption: construction foundations
open: Can a multi-key FHE scheme supporting fast evaluation allow parties to join or leave mid-computation, without redoing the upfront key aggregation or reevaluating the encrypted computation from scratch?
status: Near-single-key evaluation can rely on upfront aggregation, as in Afshar–Goyal (2026), *Multi-Key FHE Almost as Fast as Single-Key FHE*, ePrint 2026/2195; dynamic membership is a separate requirement and remains unaddressed by that approach.
solved_when: A construction exists in which keys can be added or removed as participating parties without repeating global aggregation or reevaluating the entire encrypted computation, while preserving near-single-key evaluation speed.
why: Collaborative computations need to survive participant changes; without dynamic membership, any join or leave event invalidates the aggregated-key setup and forces a full restart of the encrypted workload.
key_works: Afshar–Goyal (2026), *Multi-Key FHE Almost as Fast as Single-Key FHE*, ePrint 2026/2195.

title: Adaptive threshold FHE without idealized erasures
subfield: Fully homomorphic encryption: construction foundations
open: Can we build a fully homomorphic encryption scheme with threshold decryption that tolerates adaptive corruption, maliciously behaving decryption participants, participant dropout, and key recovery — all without assuming securely erasable local state, an assumption real implementations cannot guarantee? In other words, achieve the full operational security model for distributed FHE decryption under a standard (non-erasure) memory model.
status: Existing succinct threshold-decryption results, including Afshar–Goyal (2026), *Fully-Succinct Multi-Key FHE & Rate-1 Simulatable Threshold Decryption from LWE* (ePrint 2026/1683), do not by themselves establish this full operational security model; related work in adaptive Byzantine security and proactive secret sharing has not yet been combined with FHE to this end.
solved_when: A construction (or a proof of impossibility) is given that simultaneously handles adaptive corruption, malicious decryption, dropout, and recovery in threshold FHE, with security proven under standard assumptions such as LWE and with no reliance on secure erasure of participant state.
why: Distributed decryption is exactly the component exposed during real-world compromises and failures; without such a scheme, threshold FHE deployments lack guarantees that survive an attacker who corrupts machines mid-protocol and reads their prior state.
key_works: Afshar–Goyal (2026), *Fully-Succinct Multi-Key FHE & Rate-1 Simulatable Threshold Decryption from LWE*, ePrint 2026/1683.

title: Practical finite-block rate-1 FHE
subfield: FHE rate, native cost, numerical correctness, and implementation
open: **Proposed target:** approach unit ciphertext rate at realistic message sizes and security parameters rather than only asymptotically.
status: Rate-1 FHE already exists; the finite-block efficiency frontier remains.
why: Asymptotic compression matters only when useful workloads reach its amortization threshold.
key_works: Brakerski–Döttling–Garg–Malavolta (2019), *Leveraging Linear Decryption: Rate-1 Fully-Homomorphic Encryption and Time-Lock Puzzles*, ePrint 2019/720.

subfield: FHE rate, native cost, numerical correctness, and implementation
open: At what workload size does the total material transmitted and stored by a rate-1 FHE scheme approach the size of the plaintext itself, once evaluation keys, setup, and refresh data are counted? Formally, determine the amortization threshold at which all ciphertext-independent overhead is dominated by payload.
status: Ciphertext rate alone excludes potentially substantial overhead. Key works: Brakerski et al. (2019), *Leveraging Linear Decryption*, ePrint 2019/720.
solved_when: A quantitative analysis (or construction) identifies the workload size at which total transmitted and stored material — including evaluation keys, setup, and refresh data — approaches plaintext size.
why: It identifies when rate-1 constructions actually save resources, rather than merely shifting cost into overhead excluded from the ciphertext-rate measure.
key_works: Brakerski et al. (2019), *Leveraging Linear Decryption*, ePrint 2019/720.

title: Sustained rate across evaluated intermediates
subfield: FHE rate, native cost, numerical correctness, and implementation
open: Can fully homomorphic encryption preserve near-unit rate not just at the ciphertext output but across every intermediate value produced during evaluation, including heterogeneous chains and repeatedly reused intermediates, without hiding cost in large decompressed representations?
status: It is currently known that an encryption-rate theorem need not imply that every computation-ready intermediate has the same rate; no construction achieving sustained near-unit rate across intermediates is on record. Key works: Brakerski et al. (2019), ePrint 2019/720; Döttling–Dujmovic (2022), ePrint 2022/495.
solved_when: A scheme (or transformation) is given for which all computation-ready intermediates arising in heterogeneous evaluation chains maintain near-unit rate, with no reliance on large decompressed hidden representations.
why: Real workloads involve many intermediate encrypted objects, so a rate guarantee holding only for final outputs says little about the cost of actually running such computations.
key_works: Brakerski et al. (2019), ePrint 2019/720; Döttling–Dujmovic (2022), ePrint 2022/495.

title: Near-optimal total communication for threshold decryption
subfield: FHE rate, native cost, numerical correctness, and implementation
open: Can threshold decryption be realized so that the total communication across all participants stays near-optimal, even when each of the N decryption parties may act maliciously and robustness is required — rather than merely making each individual share small?
status: The 2026 rate-1 result (Afshar–Goyal 2026, ePrint 2026/1683) makes individual decryption shares plaintext-sized, but summing N shares still incurs an N-dependent total; no scheme yet addresses the aggregate-communication regime with malicious security and robustness.
solved_when: A threshold decryption scheme with malicious security and robustness is constructed whose total communication across all N participants is near-optimal (i.e., the summed communication no longer incurs an N-dependent blowup beyond what lower bounds dictate), ideally matching the aggregation lower bounds.
why: Per-share efficiency does not imply efficient distributed decryption: even plaintext-sized shares sum to an N-dependent total, so threshold decryption of FHE ciphertexts remains communication-prohibitive for large committees.
key_works: Afshar–Goyal (2026), ePrint 2026/1683.

title: Finite-size rate-1 quantum FHE
subfield: FHE rate, native cost, numerical correctness, and implementation
open: Can rate-1 quantum fully homomorphic encryption be made practical at finite sizes, with acceptable communication and fault-tolerant computation costs — including for non-Clifford gate evaluation?
status: Rate-1 QFHE and quantum secure function evaluation already have theoretical constructions, per Chardouvelis–Döttling–Malavolta (2020/2021), *Rate-1 Quantum Fully Homomorphic Encryption*, ePrint 2020/1454; the open problem is the finite-size, implementation-level cost regime.
solved_when: A rate-1 QFHE scheme (supporting non-Clifford evaluation) is realized with favorable finite-size communication and fault-tolerant computation costs.
why: Quantum ciphertext expansion and non-Clifford evaluation costs can dominate the practical usefulness of QFHE, so taming them is what stands between the existing theory and any real deployment.
key_works: Chardouvelis–Döttling–Malavolta (2020/2021), *Rate-1 Quantum Fully Homomorphic Encryption*, ePrint 2020/1454.

title: Boolean FHE within 10× native latency
subfield: FHE rate, native cost, numerical correctness, and implementation
open: Can fully homomorphic encryption evaluate realistic Boolean workloads at within 10× the latency of the same computation on plaintext hardware, once all required ciphertext refresh and preprocessing costs are amortized into the measurement?
status: Specialized FHE processor instructions exist, e.g. PulpFHE's complex instruction set extensions for FHE processors (Ahmed–Tsantsos-line work: Ahmed–Tsoutsos, 2024, ePrint 2024/1315), but the 10× figure is an end-to-end target, not a claimed universal record.
solved_when: A broad, publicly declared suite of Boolean workloads is evaluated end-to-end with total latency — including refresh operations and amortized preprocessing — at most 10× the matched plaintext execution latency.
why: A 10× overhead would make encrypted computation a routinely affordable option, fundamentally changing the economics of confidential computation.
key_works: Ahmed–Tsoutsos (2024), *PulpFHE: Complex Instruction Set Extensions for FHE Processors*, ePrint 2024/1315.

title: Matrix FHE within 10× native matrix computation
subfield: FHE rate, native cost, numerical correctness, and implementation
open: Can fully homomorphic encryption execute complete encrypted matrix workloads — including data movement, keys, and bootstrapping — within 10× the cost of a matched plaintext run?
status: Matrix-native bootstrapping, as in Shokri–Tsoutsos (2026), *Low-Depth Bootstrapping for Matrix-Native FHE* (ePrint 2026/811), improves specific components but does not establish near-native end-to-end execution.
solved_when: An end-to-end matrix workload runs under FHE with total cost (computation, data movement, keys, and bootstrapping) at most 10× that of the equivalent native plaintext execution.
why: Matrix computation underlies many high-value private workloads; achieving near-native encrypted performance would make such workloads practical without exposing data.
key_works: Shokri–Tsoutsos (2026), *Low-Depth Bootstrapping for Matrix-Native FHE*, ePrint 2026/811.

title: A 100× bootstrapping improvement with complete accounting
subfield: FHE rate, native cost, numerical correctness, and implementation
open: Can fully homomorphic encryption achieve a 100-fold improvement in a fixed bootstrapping benchmark — in latency or energy — while keeping security and precision identical and accounting for every cost, including preprocessing that earlier comparisons quietly omitted?
status: Existing component-level improvements do not yet constitute a universally comparable record of this kind. Related work includes Shokri–Tsoutsos (2026), *Low-Depth Bootstrapping for Matrix-Native FHE*, ePrint 2026/811.
solved_when: A fixed bootstrapping benchmark improves by 100× in latency or energy at identical security and identical precision, with complete accounting that leaves no cost hidden in omitted preprocessing, and current component improvements cohere into a universally comparable record.
why: Bootstrapping dominates the cost of most FHE workloads, so a genuine 100× gain would propagate across nearly every FHE application rather than a single niche use case.
