title: Bootstrapping with near-live-data working memory
subfield: FHE rate, native cost, numerical correctness, and implementation
open: Can fully homomorphic encryption bootstrapping be engineered so that peak working memory stays within a small multiple of the live ciphertext data being processed, rather than ballooning with the full recomputation state?
status: Memory-aware matrix-FHE systems have shown that naive representations can dominate resource use, as in Shokri–Tsoutsos (2026), *Terrazzo: Memory-Aware GPU Framework for Private Transformer Inference*, ePrint 2026/1870.
solved_when: A bootstrapping implementation is demonstrated whose peak working memory is a small constant multiple of live ciphertext data, without unacceptable cost in recomputation time or bandwidth.
why: Memory capacity and memory movement, not arithmetic, often dominate the hardware cost of FHE workloads; taming working memory directly reduces what deployment on real machines costs.
key_works: Shokri–Tsoutsos (2026), *Terrazzo: Memory-Aware GPU Framework for Private Transformer Inference*, ePrint 2026/1870.

title: Low-latency private inference without large-batch amortization
subfield: FHE rate, native cost, numerical correctness, and implementation
open: Can a fully homomorphic encryption inference system serve a single encrypted query at interactive latency, counting all per-user setup that cannot be reused across users?
status: The state of the art is Terrazzo's reported 7.04 seconds per BERT-base input, but this figure is amortized at 256-input occupancy and is not a single-query latency result.
solved_when: The declared encrypted inference workload completes at batch size one, including all non-reusable setup, within a target interactive latency; no stated numeric bound beyond "interactive," so any demonstrated single-query interactive latency for the workload qualifies.
why: Interactive users cannot always wait for a large batch, so amortized throughput results do not translate to responsive private inference.
key_works: Shokri–Tsoutsos (2026), *Terrazzo*, ePrint 2026/1870.

title: Efficient exact floating-point FHE
subfield: FHE rate, native cost, numerical correctness, and implementation
open: Can fully homomorphic encryption execute real floating-point programs with their exact specified semantics — including exceptional values, rounding modes, comparisons, and conversions — at a cost that makes practical deployment feasible, rather than silently substituting approximate arithmetic?
status: The state of the art is cross-scheme optimization, exemplified by Bian et al. (2026), *Libra: Pattern-Scheduling Co-Optimization for Cross-Scheme FHE Code Generation over GPGPU* (ePrint 2026/456); however, such optimization does not by itself establish complete floating-point semantic compatibility.
solved_when: An FHE system supports the full specified floating-point semantics (exceptional values, rounding, comparisons, and conversions) exactly, with no silent replacement by approximate arithmetic, at engineering-efficient cost.
why: It would let existing numerical software migrate to encrypted computation without changing its mathematical contract.
key_works: Bian et al. (2026), *Libra: Pattern-Scheduling Co-Optimization for Cross-Scheme FHE Code Generation over GPGPU*, ePrint 2026/456.

title: Optimal cross-scheme FHE compilation
subfield: FHE rate, native cost, numerical correctness, and implementation
open: Is there a principled way to compile a workload across fully homomorphic encryption schemes — Boolean, exact-integer, approximate-number, and matrix representations — so that end-to-end cost, including every conversion, is minimized? The goal is a compiler that jointly optimizes scheduling, conversion placement, and parameter selection while preserving provable security and end-to-end error tracking.
status: Cross-scheme compilers exist, but the joint scheduling, conversion, and parameter-selection optimum remains workload-dependent; the state of the art is represented by Bian et al. (2026), *Libra*, ePrint 2026/456.
solved_when: A compilation method exists that minimizes end-to-end cost across mixed Boolean, exact-integer, approximate-number, and matrix representations, with proven security and error tracking for all conversions.
why: No single encrypted representation is best for every operation, so the ability to move cheaply and safely among schemes determines whether a workload can run at practical cost at all.
key_works: Bian et al. (2026), *Libra*, ePrint 2026/456.

title: Low-overhead protection against approximate-decryption leakage
subfield: FHE rate, native cost, numerical correctness, and implementation
open: Can we protect approximate FHE schemes against key-recovery leakage from repeated approximate decryptions — where floating-point error acts as a side channel — while keeping useful numerical precision and low overhead even under rich adaptive queries?
status: The security distinction between exact and approximate decryption is established, and key-recovery attacks exploiting approximate-decryption leakage are known (Li–Micciancio, *On the Security of Homomorphic Encryption on Approximate Numbers*, ePrint 2020/1533, 2020/2021); practical low-cost protection under rich adaptive use remains the target.
solved_when: A protection mechanism is demonstrated that prevents key-recovery from repeated adaptive approximate decryptions, at low practical cost and without degrading the precision needed for useful approximate computation.
why: Numerical error in approximate decryption can be turned into a cryptographic side channel, so without protection, seemingly benign decryption access can leak the secret key.
key_works: Li–Micciancio (2020/2021), *On the Security of Homomorphic Encryption on Approximate Numbers*, ePrint 2020/1533.

title: Certified numerical error under adaptive encrypted computation
subfield: FHE rate, native cost, numerical correctness, and implementation
open: When an encrypted computation's later operations depend on earlier approximate outputs, can we derive useful end-to-end error bounds for the whole computation? Formally, the goal is a composable theory of certified numerical error under adaptive control flow in approximate fully homomorphic encryption.
status: Local precision estimates do not automatically compose through adaptive control flow. Key works: Li–Micciancio (2020/2021), *On the Security of Homomorphic Encryption on Approximate Numbers*, ePrint 2020/1533.
solved_when: A framework is given that yields end-to-end (not merely local) error bounds for adaptive encrypted computations, i.e., bounds that remain valid when subsequent operations depend on earlier approximate results.
why: It would make approximate encrypted computation auditable as numerical software.
key_works: Li–Micciancio (2020/2021), *On the Security of Homomorphic Encryption on Approximate Numbers*, ePrint 2020/1533.

title: Adversarially robust failure estimates
subfield: FHE rate, native cost, numerical correctness, and implementation
open: Do fully homomorphic encryption schemes remain as reliable under an adversary as under benign use — specifically, can we bound decryption and approximation failure probabilities when the adversary maliciously selects valid inputs, correlates ciphertexts, and issues repeated queries?
status: Current failure estimates assume honest random inputs; the open observation is that such estimates need not cover an adversarial deployment. Related lines include rare-event analysis and adaptive reliability bounds. Key works: Li–Micciancio (2020/2021), ePrint 2020/1533; Yang–Yu–Susilo (2025/2026), ePrint 2026/1756.
solved_when: A bound on decryption and approximation failure probability is proved that holds under maliciously chosen valid inputs, correlated ciphertexts, and repeated adaptive queries, and that meaningfully covers adversarial deployment rather than honest random-input use alone.
why: Rare failures that look negligible in honest usage may accumulate across queries or leak an exploitable attack signal, so honest estimates alone leave deployed FHE without a trustworthy reliability guarantee.
key_works: Li–Micciancio (2020/2021), ePrint 2020/1533; Yang–Yu–Susilo (2025/2026), ePrint 2026/1756.

title: Post-quantum verification below 10% of FHE evaluation cost
subfield: FHE rate, native cost, numerical correctness, and implementation
open: Can a fully homomorphic encryption evaluation be verified with a post-quantum argument of correctness that costs less than 10% of the evaluation itself? The goal is a transparent proof system whose verification overhead, relative to a declared FHE workload, stays below that threshold.
status: PRISM (Zhou–Li–Yang–Hong–Wei, 2026, ePrint 2026/1956) advances practical verification of standard RNS-based homomorphic encryption, but the stated low-overhead post-quantum target remains stronger than what is currently achieved.
solved_when: A verification scheme exists that proves correct FHE evaluation via a transparent post-quantum argument and adds less than 10% overhead to a declared evaluation workload.
why: Confidential computation should not require trusting the evaluator's answer; cheap verification would make outsourced FHE computations accountable without giving up the performance that makes them useful.
key_works: Zhou–Li–Yang–Hong–Wei (2026), *PRISM: Efficient zkSNARKs for RNS-Based Homomorphic Encryption*, ePrint 2026/1956.

title: Fast HE verification without amortized offline assumptions
subfield: FHE rate, native cost, numerical correctness, and implementation
open: Can homomorphic-encryption computations over fields and transforms be verified with proof overhead comparable to the best known amortized systems, even when the offline preparation phase cannot be reused across instances — or is adversarially generated? More precisely, is there a verification scheme for HE computations that achieves PRISM-like efficiency for cross-field and transform checks while tolerating a one-shot, untrusted offline phase?
status: The current state of the art is PRISM (Zhou et al., 2026, *PRISM*, ePrint 2026/1956), whose efficient transform-proof analysis explicitly includes an offline-phase model — i.e., its efficiency relies on that offline preparation.
solved_when: A verification scheme exists that handles cross-field and transform verification with efficiency matching the amortized offline regime, yet remains sound when the offline preparation is per-instance (no reuse) and may be produced adversarially.
why: Setup reuse and trusted offline assumptions are unrealistic in one-shot or multi-tenant deployments, so the fastest known verification techniques do not currently apply there; removing the assumption makes efficient verifiable HE usable exactly where it is most needed.
key_works: Zhou et al. (2026), *PRISM*, ePrint 2026/1956.

title: Verified constant-time FHE accelerators
subfield: FHE rate, native cost, numerical correctness, and implementation
open: Can we build a fully homomorphic encryption accelerator whose arithmetic is verified correct and whose control flow, memory accesses, and timing are proved independent of secrets, across both its hardware and software stacks?
status: Throughput-oriented instruction-set work on FHE accelerators, such as PulpFHE (Ahmed–Tsoutsos, 2024, ePrint 2024/1315), does not establish end-to-end side-channel noninterference; no existing accelerator verification covers arithmetic correctness together with constant-time behavior across the full hardware/software stack.
solved_when: A working FHE accelerator implementation, spanning hardware and software, carries a machine-checked proof of arithmetic correctness together with an end-to-end proof of secret-independent control flow, memory access patterns, and timing.
why: A fast accelerator that leaks through its microarchitecture silently invalidates the security assumptions the FHE scheme was built on, so speed gains would come at the cost of the confidentiality FHE exists to provide.

title: Predictive portable FHE cost models
subfield: FHE rate, native cost, numerical correctness, and implementation
open: Can we build a cost model that predicts the latency, memory, and energy cost of fully homomorphic encryption workloads from a single common representation of the encrypted computation, across CPUs, GPUs, and hardware accelerators?
status: Platform-specific optimization systems exist, but none provides a validated portable prediction model spanning hardware targets. Related efforts include Bian et al. (2026), *Libra*, ePrint 2026/456.
solved_when: A portable prediction model, validated against measurements on CPUs, GPUs, and accelerators, accurately forecasts latency, memory, and energy for FHE computations expressed in the common encrypted-operation representation.
why: It would let compiler optimization choices and hardware procurement decisions rest on quantitative predictions rather than trial-and-error benchmarking.
key_works: Bian et al. (2026), *Libra*, ePrint 2026/456.

title: Complete-cost replication of near-single-key multi-key FHE
subfield: FHE rate, native cost, numerical correctness, and implementation
open: Can a multi-key fully homomorphic encryption scheme match single-key FHE not just in evaluation speed but in every component of system cost — aggregation, key material, decryption, memory, and scaling with the number of participants?
status: Current claims of near-single-key performance (Afshar–Goyal (2026), *Multi-Key FHE Almost as Fast as Single-Key FHE*, ePrint 2026/2195) rest on matching evaluation cost after preprocessing; matching evaluation cost after preprocessing is not the same as matching total system cost.
solved_when: A full accounting of aggregation, key material, decryption, memory, and participant-count scaling shows total system cost at (or near) single-key levels, rather than matching evaluation cost alone after preprocessing.
why: It would identify the workloads where multi-key FHE genuinely becomes inexpensive, and expose where costs hide beyond evaluation.

title: General offline ORAM lower bounds
subfield: RAM-model MPC and oblivious memory
open: When a client can batch all its accesses in advance — the offline setting — how much can an ORAM actually reduce access overhead? We seek strong lower bounds for offline ORAM in models permitting general computation and encodings, proved directly rather than by transplanting online lower bounds into a model where they do not apply.
status: Logarithmic lower bounds are established for the online ORAM setting, but the offline case and questions about general models remain distinct and open; the Boyle–Naor (2016) work *Is There an Oblivious RAM Lower Bound?* (DOI: 10.1145/2840728.2840761) highlights the subtlety of proving such lower bounds.
solved_when: A strong lower bound on offline ORAM overhead is established in a general-computation, general-encoding model, by an argument valid in that model rather than an imported online bound.
why: It would clarify which ORAM overheads batching can fundamentally eliminate, separating what is intrinsic to obliviousness from what is an artifact of online access patterns.
key_works: Boyle–Naor (2016), *Is There an Oblivious RAM Lower Bound?*, DOI: 10.1145/2840728.2840761.

title: Joint communication–work–memory ORAM bounds
subfield: RAM-model MPC and oblivious memory
open: When an ORAM server can perform arbitrary computation on behalf of the client, what are the optimal tradeoffs among client memory, communication bandwidth, server computation, and access latency? A satisfactory answer would take the form of matching upper and lower bounds for this joint communication–work–memory–latency resource profile.
status: Known cell-probe bandwidth bounds do not automatically settle models with general server computation, so the joint tradeoff remains uncharacterized; the logarithmic lower bound machinery of Komargodski–Lin (2021/2023), *A Logarithmic Lower Bound for Oblivious RAM (For All Parameters)*, DOI: 10.1137/21M1428431, addresses the bandwidth-only setting and does not extend directly to this question.
solved_when: A characterization (tight upper and lower bounds) of the achievable tradeoff surface among client memory, communication, server computation, and latency in ORAMs with computationally capable servers.
why: Secure-memory deployments already trade bandwidth against server work, yet we lack bounds telling us when such tradeoffs are optimal — a characterization would tell designers whether current constructions leave real gains on the table.
key_works: Komargodski–Lin (2021/2023), *A Logarithmic Lower Bound for Oblivious RAM (For All Parameters)*, DOI: 10.1137/21M1428431.

title: Post-quantum garbled RAM matching DDH efficiency
subfield: RAM-model MPC and oblivious memory
open: Can a garbled RAM scheme be built entirely from post-quantum assumptions while matching the concrete efficiency of today's DDH-based constructions? Formally, this asks for a construction under ordinary post-quantum assumptions whose practical performance is comparable to PicoGRAM's DDH-based garbled RAM.
status: The state of the art, PicoGRAM (Gu–Tinoco–Rajan–Shi, 2025, ePrint 2025/1479), achieves practical garbled RAM but rests on Decisional Diffie-Hellman, which is not post-quantum; related directions include post-quantum data structures and lattice garbling.
solved_when: A garbled RAM scheme from post-quantum assumptions is exhibited whose concrete efficiency matches that of the DDH-based PicoGRAM construction.
why: It would let private RAM execution in MPC survive the failure of discrete-log assumptions once large-scale quantum computers arrive, without paying a large efficiency penalty.
key_works: Gu–Tinoco–Rajan–Shi (2025), *PicoGRAM: Practical Garbled RAM from Decisional Diffie-Hellman*, ePrint 2025/1479.

bib.title: Post-quantum garbled RAM matching DDH efficiency

title: Large-word garbled-RAM efficiency for ordinary machine words
subfield: RAM-model MPC and oblivious memory
open: Can arithmetic garbled RAM retain its communication advantages when the machine's word size is too small to absorb security-parameter costs — that is, can we give a communication accounting for ordinary (small) words matching what is known in the large-word regime?
status: Zebra (Gu–Ghoshal–Shi, 2026, *Zebra: Arithmetic Garbled RAM for Large Words from DCR*, ePrint 2026/345) explicitly targets large words; ordinary small-word regimes require separate accounting, which remains to be worked out.
solved_when: A garbled-RAM or MPC construction (or a lower-bound analysis) is given whose communication cost for standard, non-large word sizes is analyzed separately and preserves the arithmetic garbled-RAM communication advantages in that regime.
why: General-purpose software overwhelmingly manipulates short integers and pointers, so efficiency results that hold only for large words leave the practical case unaddressed.
key_works: Gu–Ghoshal–Shi (2026), *Zebra: Arithmetic Garbled RAM for Large Words from DCR*, ePrint 2026/345.

bib.title: Large-word garbled-RAM efficiency for ordinary machine words

title: Crash-consistent private RAM
subfield: RAM-model MPC and oblivious memory
open: Can a RAM-model MPC maintain a private mutable memory that survives process crashes — recovering correctly without replaying effects, losing committed writes, or leaking access patterns introduced by the recovery procedure itself?
status: Existing steady-state RAM-MPC security does not establish crash consistency; the proposed target of crash-consistent private RAM remains unachieved. Related directions include crash-consistent storage and oblivious recovery; see Falk et al. (2023), *DORAM Revisited*, ePrint 2023/578.
solved_when: A construction exists for private mutable RAM that, after a crash, recovers all committed writes, discards uncommitted effects, and preserves the obliviousness/security guarantees of steady-state RAM-MPC throughout recovery.
why: Real deployments face ordinary operational failures; without crash consistency, private computation cannot be trusted to survive them, since steady-state security guarantees simply do not cover the recovery path.
key_works: Falk et al. (2023), *DORAM Revisited*, ePrint 2023/578.

title: Fully private encrypted-RAM delegation
subfield: RAM-model MPC and oblivious memory
open: Can encrypted-RAM delegation be made fully private, so that a delegation of computation on encrypted memory reveals neither the data nor the program being executed nor its access pattern? Formally, this asks for a strengthening of the existing partially hiding eRAM notion in which the program and access-pattern information are hidden as well, with an explicit leakage profile and succinctness guarantees.
status: The 2024–2025 eRAM framework of Afshar–Cheng–Goyal–Yadav–Yadugiri (Encrypted RAM Delegation, ePrint 2024/1806) supplies powerful applications but only achieves a distinguishing notion of partial hiding; full hiding of the program and access pattern remains open.
solved_when: A delegation scheme is constructed that achieves the existing eRAM framework's succinctness and applications while hiding the desired program and access-pattern information, with the leakage made explicit.
why: Data owners delegating computation on encrypted RAM may need to conceal not just their data but which program is run on it — partial hiding leaves this exposed.
key_works: Afshar–Cheng–Goyal–Yadav–Yadugiri (2024/2025), *Encrypted RAM Delegation*, ePrint 2024/1806.

title: Key-homomorphic RAM computation from plain LWE
subfield: RAM-model MPC and oblivious memory
open: Can succinct key-homomorphic computation for RAM programs be based on ordinary LWE rather than decomposed LWE, without losing the encoding efficiency that makes the framework useful?
status: The state of the art is the 2025 construction of Abram–Malavolta–Roy (*Key-Homomorphic Computations for RAM: Fully Succinct Randomised Encodings and More*, ePrint 2025/339), which achieves the goal but under the stronger assumption of decomposed LWE.
solved_when: A construction of succinct key-homomorphic RAM computation (e.g., fully succinct randomized encodings) is proved secure under plain LWE while retaining the encoding efficiency of the 2025 construction.
why: It would put a powerful RAM-computation framework on a cleaner, more standard foundation, removing the need for the stronger decomposed-LWE assumption.
key_works: Abram–Malavolta–Roy (2025), *Key-Homomorphic Computations for RAM: Fully Succinct Randomised Encodings and More*, ePrint 2025/339.

bib.title: Key-homomorphic RAM computation from plain LWE

title: Work- and span-efficient private PRAM
subfield: RAM-model MPC and oblivious memory
open: Can a data-dependent PRAM program be executed securely while preserving both its total work and its parallel depth (span), rather than forcing it into a sequential simulation?
status: It is known that efficient sequential RAM simulation does not automatically preserve useful parallelism. Related work includes Abram–Malavolta–Roy (2025), ePrint 2025/339.
solved_when: A secure simulation of arbitrary data-dependent parallel RAM programs exists that matches the original program's work and span up to constant (or otherwise explicitly bounded) factors.
why: Sequentializing private computation forfeits the speedups available from multicore and distributed hardware, so private execution of parallel programs currently pays for privacy with the loss of parallelism itself.
key_works: Abram–Malavolta–Roy (2025), ePrint 2025/339.

title: Oblivious dynamic allocation and resizing
subfield: RAM-model MPC and oblivious memory
open: Can we build an oblivious heap that supports private allocation, deallocation, resizing, and sparse objects, without leaking object lifetimes or forcing a reconstruction of the entire memory?
status: Fixed-array private memory does not by itself provide a secure heap. Related directions include dynamic-memory lower bounds and garbage collection; see Gu et al. (2025), *PicoGRAM*, ePrint 2025/1479, and Gu–Ghoshal–Shi (2026), *Zebra*, ePrint 2026/345.
solved_when: A scheme exists supporting allocation, deallocation, resizing, and sparse objects with no leakage of lifetimes and no full-memory reconstruction requirement.
why: General-purpose programs depend on dynamic memory, so secure computation that only offers fixed arrays cannot run them naturally.
key_works: Gu et al. (2025), *PicoGRAM*, ePrint 2025/1479; Gu–Ghoshal–Shi (2026), *Zebra*, ePrint 2026/345.

title: Succinct HSS beyond linear usage
subfield: Homomorphic secret sharing, garbling, and preprocessing
open: Can succinct homomorphic secret sharing be extended from read-once programs to general programs that reuse inputs and intermediate values? Formally, is there a succinct HSS scheme supporting non-linear input usage while preserving succinct sharing and efficient homomorphic evaluation?
status: The 2024 succinct construction of Abram–Roy–Scholl (2024), *Succinct Homomorphic Secret Sharing* (ePrint 2024/814), explicitly exploits restricted (read-once) input usage, and no construction is known beyond that setting.
solved_when: A succinct HSS construction is given that supports general (non-read-once) input usage across evaluation, while retaining succinct input sharing and efficient evaluation.
why: Real programs routinely reuse values and intermediate results, so the read-once restriction blocks application of succinct HSS to general computation.
key_works: Abram–Roy–Scholl (2024), *Succinct Homomorphic Secret Sharing*, ePrint 2024/814.

title: Rate-1 arithmetic garbling without KDM assumptions
subfield: Homomorphic secret sharing, garbling, and preprocessing
open: Can rate-1 arithmetic garbling be achieved under standard assumptions, without key-dependent-message security for messages involving keys and inverses? More precisely, can the strongest known rate parameters for arithmetic garbling be obtained without any KDM assumption?
status: The 2024 construction of Meyer–Orlandi–Roy–Scholl (*Rate-1 Arithmetic Garbling from Homomorphic Secret-Sharing*, ePrint 2024/820) achieves the strongest rate-1 parameters, but separates assumption-dependent rates: ordinary IND-CPA security does not automatically yield the strongest rate, so the current best constructions rely on the stronger KDM-style assumptions.
solved_when: A garbling scheme for arithmetic computations achieves the strongest rate-1 parameters of Meyer–Orlandi–Roy–Scholl (2024) while assuming only ordinary IND-CPA security, with no KDM assumptions involving keys and inverses.
why: It would remove a specialized, nonstandard assumption from the foundation of highly communication-efficient secure computation, making rate-1 garbling usable wherever plain semantic security is already trusted.
key_works: Meyer–Orlandi–Roy–Scholl (2024), *Rate-1 Arithmetic Garbling from Homomorphic Secret-Sharing*, ePrint 2024/820.

bib.title: Rate-1 arithmetic garbling without KDM assumptions

title: Information-theoretic publicly verifiable secret-sharing deletion
subfield: Homomorphic secret sharing, garbling, and preprocessing
open: Can secret sharing be made information-theoretically secure while allowing anyone at all — not just the participating parties — to verify that the secret has been deleted? Formally, construct an information-theoretic secret-sharing scheme with publicly verifiable deletion, replacing the current requirement of unanimous verification by the relevant participants.
status: The 2026 unanimously verifiable construction explicitly leaves public verification as a stronger target (Chen–Ji–Luo, 2026, *Linearly Homomorphic Secret Sharing and Multi-Party Computation with Unanimously Verifiable Deletion*, ePrint 2026/1673). No information-theoretic publicly verifiable deletion construction is known.
solved_when: A construction is given of information-theoretic secret sharing whose deletion can be verified by any party without secret verification information, in contrast to schemes where verification requires unanimity among the participants.
why: Public verification removes the need to trust the participants: any external party could confirm deletion without holding secret verification information, which the existing unanimously verifiable construction explicitly cannot offer.
key_works: Chen–Ji–Luo (2026), *Linearly Homomorphic Secret Sharing and Multi-Party Computation with Unanimously Verifiable Deletion*, ePrint 2026/1673.

title: Verifiable-deletion MPC with malicious clients
subfield: Homomorphic secret sharing, garbling, and preprocessing
open: Can the deletion-capable outsourced MPC functionality be extended to handle malicious clients, while keeping both its security against quantum servers and its useful efficiency?
status: The 2026 construction (Chen–Ji–Luo, ePrint 2026/1673) distinguishes semi-honest clients from malicious quantum servers, leaving malicious-client security unaddressed.
solved_when: A construction realizes the deletion-capable outsourced MPC functionality against malicious clients (in addition to malicious quantum servers), preserving the quantum-server security and efficiency profile of the existing scheme.
why: Without this, clients can supply malformed shares or manipulate deletion obligations, undermining the integrity of the deletion guarantee.
key_works: Chen–Ji–Luo (2026), ePrint 2026/1673.

title: Constant-rate SFE without obfuscation
subfield: Homomorphic secret sharing, garbling, and preprocessing
open: Can any interactive protocol be compiled into a secure function evaluation scheme whose communication is only a constant factor larger than the protocol's own communication, without invoking indistinguishability obfuscation? Formally, is there such a compiler based on assumptions strictly weaker than iO?
status: A 2026 compiler achieves constant rate, but it relies on input-succinct Turing-machine obfuscation, with additional setup-model variants [Pandey–Smith–Tang (2026), *Communication Preserving SFE from Obfuscation*, ePrint 2026/2214]; the question of achieving this without obfuscation remains open.
solved_when: A compiler from arbitrary interactive protocols to secure function evaluation is constructed that achieves constant communication rate and is proven secure under assumptions weaker than iO.
why: It would remove the polynomial-in-security-parameter communication overhead that current secure computation imposes, making security essentially free in terms of bandwidth.
key_works: Pandey–Smith–Tang (2026), *Communication Preserving SFE from Obfuscation*, ePrint 2026/2214.

title: Tight function-dependence bounds for MPC preprocessing
subfield: Homomorphic secret sharing, garbling, and preprocessing
open: Which parts of secure-computation preprocessing must be tailored to the function being computed, and which can depend only on its size, or on neither? A satisfactory answer would characterize the minimal degree of function dependence, with matching upper bounds (efficient constructions) and lower bounds on efficiency and leakage.
status: A 2026 systematization by Brüggemann–Edalatnejad–Filipp–Kusterer–Schneider (*It’s Not Just a Phase: Understanding Function Dependence in MPC Preprocessing*, ePrint 2026/2029) distinguishes several forms of function dependence; a complete quantitative frontier remains to be established.
solved_when: A quantitative frontier is established: for each form of function dependence, matching efficiency and leakage lower bounds, so that every preprocessing component is classified as needing dependence on the function, its size, or neither, tightly.
why: It tells us whether reusable, function-independent preprocessing is achievable — which would substantially reduce the cost of repeated private computations.
key_works: Brüggemann–Edalatnejad–Filipp–Kusterer–Schneider (2026), *It’s Not Just a Phase: Understanding Function Dependence in MPC Preprocessing*, ePrint 2026/2029.

bib.title: Tight function-dependence bounds for MPC preprocessing

title: Fully adaptive NP SNARGs from plain LWE
subfield: SNARG and SNARK foundations
open: Can we construct standard-model succinct non-interactive arguments (SNARGs) for all of NP with fully adaptive soundness, assuming only ordinary polynomially hard LWE? That is, can plain LWE — with no extra assumptions or structural augmentation — serve as the sole foundation for fully adaptively sound NP SNARGs in the standard model?
status: The current state of the art is the 2026 non-black-box result of Jin–Lu–Peng (2026), *SNARKs from LWE via Non-black-Box Reductions*, DOI: 10.1145/3798129.3800888, which achieves SNARKs from LWE but with qualifications: its reach is limited to UP rather than all NP, and its provability and soundness properties come with caveats.
solved_when: A construction of standard-model SNARGs for all NP is given whose fully adaptive soundness reduces to polynomially hard plain LWE, with no qualifications on the soundness (e.g., no restriction to UP languages or reliance on provability conditions).
why: It would ground general succinct verification for all NP in a conventional, well-studied post-quantum assumption, removing the need for stronger or less standard hypotheses.
key_works: Jin–Lu–Peng (2026), *SNARKs from LWE via Non-black-Box Reductions*, DOI: 10.1145/3798129.3800888.

bib.title: Fully adaptive NP SNARGs from plain LWE

title: Almost-everywhere soundness for non-black-box LWE SNARKs
subfield: SNARG and SNARK foundations
open: Can the LWE-based SNARK construction of Jin–Lu–Peng be proved sound not just for infinitely many parameters, but for all sufficiently large parameters? Formally, can the infinitely-often soundness of their non-black-box reduction be strengthened to eventual (almost-everywhere) soundness?
status: The 2026 theorem of Jin–Lu–Peng (*SNARKs from LWE via Non-black-Box Reductions*, DOI: 10.1145/3798129.3800888) establishes soundness only on an infinite subset of parameters; this infinitely-often character is a substantive limitation, and the gap between infinitely-often and eventual hardness remains open.
solved_when: A proof (or refutation) of soundness for the Jin–Lu–Peng LWE SNARK construction at all sufficiently large security parameters, replacing the current infinitely-often guarantee.
why: Infinitely-often soundness leaves long stretches of insecure parameters, whereas real deployments must choose concrete parameters and need security exactly there.
key_works: Jin–Lu–Peng (2026), *SNARKs from LWE via Non-black-Box Reductions*, DOI: 10.1145/3798129.3800888.

bib.title: Almost-everywhere soundness for non-black-box LWE SNARKs

title: Constructively parameterized CRS lengths
subfield: SNARG and SNARK foundations
open: Can the nonconstructive parameter selection in the non-black-box LWE SNARK be replaced by an explicit, efficiently computable rule for CRS lengths that works uniformly for all security parameters?
status: The 2026 construction of Jin–Lu–Peng (DOI: 10.1145/3798129.3800888) achieves a non-black-box LWE SNARK, but its setup qualification involves nonconstructive parameter selection; this is not merely an implementation detail but a gap in the theorem itself.
solved_when: The Jin–Lu–Peng (2026) construction admits a CRS-length rule that is efficiently specified and uniformly usable, with a proof that it preserves the construction's security for every security parameter, eliminating the nonconstructive setup qualification.
why: Without an effective way to identify usable security parameters, the theorem behind the SNARK cannot support actual deployment; constructive parameter selection is what makes the security guarantee usable in practice.

title: Repairing the nonsignaling-PCP route after the AND-code refutation
subfield: SNARG and SNARK foundations
open: What encoding or proof-norm framework can replace the refuted AND-code hypothesis and make the nonsignaling-PCP route to SNARGs for NP go through? More precisely, is there an alternative encoding, constraint system, or norm-based soundness argument that supports the intended SNARG construction?
status: A May 2026 preprint (Jin 2026, *Low-Norm Nullstellensatz Hypothesis for the AND Code is False*, ePrint 2026/1087) gives exponential lower bounds refuting the proposed low-norm Nullstellensatz hypothesis; that original conjecture is therefore not retained as open. The construction it was meant to support is from Devadas et al. (2026), *SNARGs for NP and Non-Signaling PCPs, Revisited*, ePrint 2026/006.
solved_when: A construction and proof are given — an alternative encoding, constraint system, or proof-norm argument supporting the intended SNARG construction without relying on the refuted low-norm Nullstellensatz hypothesis for the AND code.
why: It isolates a concrete mathematical repair problem for a central route to SNARGs for NP, rather than letting the program rest on a lemma now known to be false.
key_works: Devadas et al. (2026), *SNARGs for NP and Non-Signaling PCPs, Revisited*, ePrint 2026/006; Jin (2026), *Low-Norm Nullstellensatz Hypothesis for the AND Code is False*, ePrint 2026/1087.

bib.title: Repairing the nonsignaling-PCP route after the AND-code refutation

title: Removing efficiently provable witness uniqueness
subfield: SNARG and SNARK foundations
open: Can the recent non-black-box SNARK construction for LWE be extended to NP relations beyond those with efficiently provable witness uniqueness? Formally, can the approach — which currently applies to UP-style relations admitting polynomial-size Extended Frege uniqueness proofs — handle relations that naturally admit many witnesses?
status: The state of the art is the Jin–Lu–Peng (2026) non-black-box SNARK approach (DOI: 10.1145/3798129.3800888), which relies on the relation having an efficiently provable uniqueness property; polynomial-size Extended Frege uniqueness proofs are a meaningful restriction on the class of relations covered.
solved_when: A non-black-box LWE-based SNARK is constructed for a class of NP relations strictly larger than UP relations with efficiently provable (Extended Frege, polynomial-size) uniqueness proofs.
why: Most NP relations of interest naturally have many witnesses, so the current restriction to efficiently provable uniqueness leaves the construction far from covering general NP; removing it would make the SNARK applicable to realistic relations.

title: The optimal CRS-length frontier
subfield: SNARG and SNARK foundations
open: What is the minimum common reference string (CRS) length for which succinct arguments remain possible, once adaptivity, uniformity, the class of languages, and the reduction model are all fixed? A complete answer would match constructive upper bounds with matching impossibility lower bounds along each of these axes simultaneously.
status: Recent short-CRS barriers — notably Chen–Jin (2025), *On the Impossibility of SNARGs with Short CRS (or: Revisiting Gentry-Wichs Barrier in the Non-adaptive Setting)*, FOCS 2025 — show that setup size cannot be treated as incidental, but the full frontier remains unmapped.
solved_when: For each setting of the parameters (adaptive vs. non-adaptive, uniform vs. non-uniform, language class, reduction model), there exist constructions whose CRS length matches a proven lower bound of the same form.
why: It determines which reusable succinct setups for SNARGs and SNARKs are actually attainable, telling designers whether short-CRS systems can exist or must instead amortize or distribute setup costs.
key_works: Chen–Jin (2025), *On the Impossibility of SNARGs with Short CRS (or: Revisiting Gentry-Wichs Barrier in the Non-adaptive Setting)*, FOCS 2025.

title: Standard-model transparent succinct arguments from hashes
subfield: SNARG and SNARK foundations
open: Can general-purpose transparent succinct arguments be built from conventional hash assumptions alone, in the standard model, with no programmable random oracle — even allowing non-black-box techniques?
status: Transparent hash-based systems exist, but transparency does not remove the random-oracle idealization or the extraction barriers; related work includes Chen–Jin (2025), *On the Impossibility of SNARGs with Short CRS*, and Devadas et al. (2026), ePrint 2026/006.
solved_when: A construction of general transparent succinct arguments is given whose security rests only on standard assumptions about hash functions, without random-oracle idealization or programmability.
why: It would place a major proof-system architecture on standard cryptographic foundations rather than heuristic random-oracle modeling.
key_works: Chen–Jin (2025), *On the Impossibility of SNARGs with Short CRS*; Devadas et al. (2026), ePrint 2026/006.

bib.title: Standard-model transparent succinct arguments from hashes

title: Publicly verifiable NIZKs for QMA
subfield: SNARG and SNARK foundations
open: Can we build a noninteractive zero-knowledge proof system for QMA statements whose proofs anyone can check, rather than only a designated verifier? A construction should come with a clearly specified setup model (common reference string, quantum preprocessing, or otherwise) and explicit, precisely stated assumptions.
status: The classical Fiat–Shamir transform does not directly handle quantum first messages, and recent generic-compiler barriers have sharpened the difficulty of removing interaction. Spooner–Tromanhauser (2026), *On Removing Interaction from Quantum Proofs*, ePrint 2026/1795, is a key recent work.
solved_when: A publicly verifiable noninteractive zero-knowledge proof (or argument) for QMA is constructed and proved both zero-knowledge and sound under explicitly stated assumptions in a precisely defined setup model.
why: It would let classical third parties verify quantum evidence — for example, quantum computation claims — without any interaction with the prover, enabling auditability wherever quantum witnesses are involved.
key_works: Spooner–Tromanhauser (2026), *On Removing Interaction from Quantum Proofs*, ePrint 2026/1795.

title: Structured quantum Fiat–Shamir beyond generic barriers
subfield: SNARG and SNARK foundations
open: Are there natural structured classes of quantum interactive proofs for which the Fiat–Shamir transformation — replacing interaction with a random oracle — can be proven sound, even though fully generic compilers are impossible? A satisfactory answer would characterize such a class and exhibit an interaction-removal procedure that is sound within it.
status: Spooner–Tromanhauser (2026), *On Removing Interaction from Quantum Proofs*, ePrint 2026/1795, establish a barrier: the excluded generic transformation class would imply QMA = BQP, so broad generic compilers cannot be hoped for.
solved_when: A nontrivial structured class of quantum protocols is identified, together with a proof that removing interaction for protocols in the class preserves soundness; conversely, progress could also show which structure is provably necessary given the 2026 generic barrier.
why: It tells constructors where sound Fiat–Shamir-style compilers can actually exist, steering effort away from the generic setting that is now ruled out and toward special cases that may yield post-quantum SNARGs and SNARKs.
key_works: Spooner–Tromanhauser (2026), *On Removing Interaction from Quantum Proofs*, ePrint 2026/1795.

bib.title: Structured quantum Fiat–Shamir beyond generic barriers

title: Tight recursive QROM extraction with quantum advice
subfield: SNARG and SNARK foundations
open: Can Fiat–Shamir proofs that are reused recursively — across adaptive statements, many sessions, and adversaries holding entangled quantum advice — be proven tightly secure in the quantum random oracle model? A tight reduction is wanted for the full recursive stack, not merely for each individual round of reprogramming.
status: The 2026 multi-reprogramming theorem of Huang–Liao (*Multi-Reprogramming with Quantum Advice in the Quantum Random Oracle Model*, ePrint 2026/2140) improves an important tool, but it does not automatically certify every recursive proof stack.
solved_when: A theorem certifies tight security for recursively composed Fiat–Shamir proofs under adaptive statements, many sessions, and quantum advice, covering the entire recursive proof stack.
why: Loose or incomplete reductions can erase the concrete post-quantum security margins of deployed proof systems.
key_works: Huang–Liao (2026), *Multi-Reprogramming with Quantum Advice in the Quantum Random Oracle Model*, ePrint 2026/2140.

title: Exact mutual-correlated-agreement parameters
subfield: Coding theory and practical transparent post-quantum proofs
open: What is the largest proximity radius for which mutual correlated agreement holds for the specified Reed–Solomon families at a concrete error target such as \(2^{-128}\)? Equivalently, determine the exact admissible-agreement parameters that a transparent proof system may rely on at fixed, cryptographic-size parameters.
status: Current results give fixed-slack asymptotic advances, but these do not identify the largest safe radius at finite parameters; the exact finite-parameter answer remains open. See Arnon–Boneh–Fenzi (2026), *Open Problems in List Decoding and Correlated Agreement*, ePrint 2026/680.
solved_when: The largest admissible proximity radius is determined explicitly for the specified Reed–Solomon families at an error target such as \(2^{-128}\), replacing fixed-slack asymptotic bounds with exact finite-parameter values.
why: Exact parameters would let transparent post-quantum proofs reduce their query complexity, tightening security analyses without resorting to speculative assumptions.
key_works: Arnon–Boneh–Fenzi (2026), *Open Problems in List Decoding and Correlated Agreement*, ePrint 2026/680.
prize: Eligible work falls within the official **$1 million Proximity Prize pool**, subject to its conditions; this is not an individual guaranteed award.

title: Exact interleaved-list-decoding challenge
subfield: Coding theory and practical transparent post-quantum proofs
open: For the Reed–Solomon families designated by the Proximity Prize, how far can one push the decoding radius of interleaved list-decoding at constant interleaving order while keeping the list size bounded? Formally, determine the maximal decoding radius for which interleaved Reed–Solomon codes admit list-decoding with the specified list-size bound.
status: This is posed as a distinct quantitative challenge from mutual correlated agreement. The problem appears in Arnon–Boneh–Fenzi (2026), *Open Problems in List Decoding and Correlated Agreement*, ePrint 2026/680, and carries an award from the same $1 million Proximity Prize pool under the published eligibility and award rules.
solved_when: A proof pins down the exact maximal decoding radius for constant interleaving order meeting the specified list-size requirements in the Proximity Prize's Reed–Solomon families, either by an achievable scheme or by a matching upper bound.
why: A solution upgrades a central coding-theoretic ingredient of transparent post-quantum proofs, directly improving the parameters these proof systems can achieve.
key_works: Arnon–Boneh–Fenzi (2026), *Open Problems in List Decoding and Correlated Agreement*, ePrint 2026/680.
prize: Part of the same **$1 million Proximity Prize pool**, under the published eligibility and award rules.

title: Bit-efficient Reed–Solomon decoding near capacity
subfield: Coding theory and practical transparent post-quantum proofs
open: Can Reed–Solomon codes be list-decoded (with fixed slack) up to capacity in time polynomial in the block length \(n\) and \(\log q\), rather than polynomial in the field size \(q\)? Formally, the goal is bit-efficient decoding guarantees matching the known near-capacity decoding guarantees, with running time \(\mathrm{poly}(n, \log q)\).
status: A September 2026 preprint (Jeronjo, *Algorithmic List Decoding at Capacity and Optimal Proximity Gaps for Reed–Solomon Codes*, arXiv:2609.05870) reports fixed-slack prime-field decoding with \(q^{O_\gamma(1)}\) running time — polynomial in \(q\), not \(\log q\), so the bit-efficiency target remains open.
solved_when: A fixed-slack near-capacity decoding algorithm for Reed–Solomon codes runs in time polynomial in \(n\) and \(\log q\), with no dependence polynomial in \(q\).
why: Polynomial-in-\(q\) algorithms become unusable over the large fields needed for cryptographic applications, in particular practical transparent post-quantum proof systems; a bit-efficient decoder would make near-capacity Reed–Solomon decoding implementable in that setting.
key_works: Jeronimo (2026), *Algorithmic List Decoding at Capacity and Optimal Proximity Gaps for Reed–Solomon Codes*, arXiv:2609.05870.

title: Shrinking-slack proximity-gap tradeoffs
subfield: Coding theory and practical transparent post-quantum proofs
open: How do list-size and agreement bounds behave when the gap to capacity shrinks with the block length, instead of staying fixed? Formally, determine the tight list-size and agreement parameters in this shrinking-slack regime.
status: Positive results exist for fixed slack, but counterexamples show failure near capacity, and these parameter regimes must not be conflated. Key works: Jeronimo (2026), arXiv:2609.05870; Krachun–Kazanin–Haböck (2026), *Failure of Proximity Gaps Close to Capacity*, ePrint 2026/782.
solved_when: Tight list-size and agreement bounds are established for proximity gaps whose distance to capacity shrinks with block length, matching the known upper and lower bounds in that regime.
why: Practical transparent post-quantum proof systems push for rates close to capacity, where the fixed-slack guarantees no longer apply; without tight bounds there, the soundness parameters of these systems rest on unverified assumptions.
key_works: Jeronimo (2026), arXiv:2609.05870; Krachun–Kazanin–Haböck (2026), *Failure of Proximity Gaps Close to Capacity*, ePrint 2026/782.

title: Sound small-characteristic code regimes after counterexamples
subfield: Coding theory and practical transparent post-quantum proofs
open: Which families of small-characteristic extension codes, and in which parameter ranges, actually support the list-size and distance-preservation bounds needed for practical transparent proofs — now that optimistic blanket assumptions over small fields have failed? A precise characterization would delimit where small-field proof systems remain sound.
status: Recent attacks show that optimistic blanket small-field assumptions are false; see Fenzi–Sanso (2025/2026), *Small-field Hash-based SNARGs Are Less Sound Than Conjectured*, ePrint 2025/2197.
solved_when: A characterization exists of the small-characteristic extension-code families and parameter ranges for which sufficiently strong list-size and distance-preservation bounds provably hold.
why: Small fields promise fast, practical transparent post-quantum proofs, but working over them can silently change the soundness calculation; without sound regimes, deployments built on small-field assumptions rest on false conjectures.
key_works: Fenzi–Sanso (2025/2026), *Small-field Hash-based SNARGs Are Less Sound Than Conjectured*, ePrint 2025/2197.

title: Sharp concrete FRI soundness beyond classical thresholds
subfield: Coding theory and practical transparent post-quantum proofs
open: Can we prove, with fully explicit constants, the concrete soundness of FRI when its parameters are pushed past the classical Johnson-bound regime — so that practitioners can verify security rather than trust conjectures? Formally, the goal is finite-parameter soundness bounds with explicit constants, query counts, and composition losses in useful beyond-Johnson regimes.
status: A 2026 preprint by Chai–Fan, *FRI Soundness Above the Johnson Bound via Threshold Halving* (ePrint 2026/858), proposes threshold-halving bounds; practical optimality and complete-stack calibration remain separate obligations.
solved_when: Independently checkable soundness bounds exist for finite parameters, with explicit constants, query counts, and composition losses stated for beyond-Johnson regimes.
why: It would replace conjectural soundness estimates with auditable security parameters for transparent post-quantum proof systems.
key_works: Chai–Fan (2026), *FRI Soundness Above the Johnson Bound via Threshold Halving*, ePrint 2026/858.

title: Sub-10-kilobyte lattice polynomial commitments
subfield: Coding theory and practical transparent post-quantum proofs
open: Can a lattice-based polynomial commitment scheme produce proofs under 10 KB for substantial polynomial sizes while matching the post-quantum security of current schemes, counting auxiliary proofs and setup in the budget?
status: The state of the art is Akita (Dao et al., 2026, *Akita: A High-Performance Lattice-Based Polynomial Commitment Scheme*, ePrint 2026/1983), which reports proofs of approximately 61–72 KB in its evaluated configurations. Related directions include lattice compression and succinct linear-algebra proofs.
solved_when: A transparent lattice polynomial commitment scheme achieves proofs below 10 KB for substantial polynomial commitments at matched post-quantum security, with auxiliary proofs and setup included in the size count.
why: It would narrow a key usability gap between lattice-based and pairing-based proof systems, where the proof sizes currently differ by an order of magnitude.
key_works: Dao et al. (2026), *Akita: A High-Performance Lattice-Based Polynomial Commitment Scheme*, ePrint 2026/1983.

title: Efficient polylogarithmic verification for lattice commitments
subfield: Coding theory and practical transparent post-quantum proofs
open: Can a lattice-based commitment scheme achieve verification time that is genuinely polylogarithmic in the computation size, with practical constants and near-linear proving time, while keeping proofs compact?
status: The current state of the art is Akita (Dao et al., 2026, ePrint 2026/1983), which offers tunable \(N^{1/K}\)-type verification for fixed \(K\); this is not the same as a practical polylogarithmic bound.
solved_when: A lattice commitment scheme is constructed whose verification complexity is polylogarithmic (not merely \(N^{1/K}\) for fixed \(K\)), with practical constants, near-linear proving time, and compact proofs.
why: Without it, verifiers become the bottleneck as committed computations grow, undermining the purpose of succinct post-quantum proofs in practice.
key_works: Dao et al. (2026), *Akita*, ePrint 2026/1983.

title: Tiny fully post-quantum recursive proofs
subfield: Coding theory and practical transparent post-quantum proofs
open: Can we build recursively composable proof systems whose proofs stay below roughly one kilobyte, with practical proving and verification, while remaining fully post-quantum — i.e., with no pairing-based wrapper in the final step? The target is a fully post-quantum tiny-proof system with efficient recursion.
status: Post-quantum small-field folding exists, via Nguyen–Setty (2026), *Neo and SuperNeo: Post-quantum Folding with Pay-per-bit Costs over Small Fields* (ePrint 2026/242), but the complete tiny-proof target — recursion below a kilobyte without pairing-based wrapping — remains stronger than what is currently achieved.
solved_when: A recursively composable, fully post-quantum proof system is constructed whose proofs are below roughly one kilobyte, with practical proving and verification times, and no pairing-based final wrapper.
why: It would make long proof histories cheap to transmit and verify, unlocking lightweight proof-carrying data and recursive verification at scale.
key_works: Nguyen–Setty (2026), *Neo and SuperNeo: Post-quantum Folding with Pay-per-bit Costs over Small Fields*, ePrint 2026/242.

title: Optimal streamed-prover time–space tradeoffs
subfield: Coding theory and practical transparent post-quantum proofs
open: What are the best possible tradeoffs between prover time and prover memory for proof systems on computations whose witnesses can be generated in small space, when stream generation, rereads, and commitment work are all counted?
status: Hobbit (Pappas–Papadopoulos 2025, ePrint 2025/1214) already achieves optimal prover time in its model; any stronger memory bounds must not omit the cost of supplying the stream.
solved_when: A proof system (or a matching lower bound) is given whose prover time and memory are optimal in a model that explicitly accounts for the cost of supplying the witness stream, including rereads and commitment computations.
why: Without such accounting, large proofs silently rely on unaccounted execution-trace storage, undermining the space-efficiency the constructions claim.
key_works: Pappas–Papadopoulos (2025), *Hobbit: Space-Efficient zkSNARK with Optimal Prover Time*, ePrint 2025/1214.

title: OWFs from \(P\neq NP\)
subfield: Minimal assumptions, meta-complexity, and remaining post-quantum constructions
open: Can one-way functions be derived from the sole assumption that \(P\neq NP\), with no additional average-case hardness assumption? Formally, this asks for a worst-case-to-average-case reduction that converts worst-case NP hardness into average-case one-wayness.
status: Modern meta-complexity characterizations, notably Liu–Pass (2020), *On One-Way Functions and Kolmogorov Complexity* (DOI: 10.1109/FOCS46700.2020.00118) and Liu–Pass (2026) (DOI: 10.4230/LIPIcs.ITCS.2026.97), sharpen the gap between worst-case and average-case hardness but do not remove it.
solved_when: A construction of a one-way function is given whose security reduces to \(P\neq NP\) (worst-case NP hardness) alone.
why: It would connect the most basic cryptographic primitive to the central conjecture of complexity theory, anchoring cryptography in worst-case hardness.
key_works: Liu–Pass (2020), *On One-Way Functions and Kolmogorov Complexity*, DOI: 10.1109/FOCS46700.2020.00118; Liu–Pass (2026), DOI: 10.4230/LIPIcs.ITCS.2026.97.

title: Post-quantum OWFs from quantum worst-case hardness
subfield: Minimal assumptions, meta-complexity, and remaining post-quantum constructions
open: Derive classical functions hard to invert quantumly from a natural worst-case assumption such as appropriate NP hardness against quantum computation, without quantum iO.
status: Quantum-iO-based implications do not establish the bare worst-case implication.
why: It would give a foundational explanation for post-quantum cryptography.
key_works: Morimae–Shirakawa–Yamakawa (2025/2026), arXiv:2506.19542.

title: Classical key agreement from OWFs beyond black-box methods
subfield: Minimal assumptions, meta-complexity, and remaining post-quantum constructions
open: Can classical key agreement be constructed from one-way functions using non-black-box techniques? Or is there a barrier showing that such constructions are impossible even beyond the black-box setting?
status: The foundational 1989 black-box separation of Impagliazzo–Rudich (*Limits on the Provable Consequences of One-Way Permutations*, DOI: 10.1145/73007.73012) remains compatible with unresolved non-black-box possibilities; Barnum–Heath (2026), ePrint 2026/113, is a key recent work on the problem.
solved_when: Either an explicit classical key agreement scheme is built from one-way functions via non-black-box techniques, or a stronger separation is established ruling out such constructions beyond black-box reductions.
why: This question marks a central boundary between symmetric-key and public-key cryptography — essentially the Minicrypt-versus-Cryptomania divide — and resolving it would clarify the minimal assumptions underlying public-key primitives.
key_works: Impagliazzo–Rudich (1989), *Limits on the Provable Consequences of One-Way Permutations*, DOI: 10.1145/73007.73012; Barnum–Heath (2026), ePrint 2026/113.

title: Standard-model oblivious interactive hashing from OWFs
subfield: Minimal assumptions, meta-complexity, and remaining post-quantum constructions
open: Construct the oblivious interactive hash primitive from OWFs in the standard model.
status: The 2026 work constructs it from random oracles and from OT, and derives OT non-black-box from a standard-model instance; it does not construct OT from a random oracle.
why: It offers a sharply formulated intermediate target for crossing classical cryptographic boundaries.
key_works: Barnum–Heath (2026), *How to Steal Oblivious Transfer from Minicrypt*, ePrint 2026/113.

title: Monotone distributional collision resistance from dCRH
subfield: Minimal assumptions, meta-complexity, and remaining post-quantum constructions
open: Can monotone distributional collision-resistant hash functions be constructed from ordinary distributional collision-resistant hashes alone, without assuming full collision resistance? Formally, the goal is a construction whose only assumption is dCRH.
status: The 2026 result (Puniamurthy (2026), *A Note on the Existence of Monotone Distributional Collision Resistant Hash Functions*, IACR CiC 3(1), article 11) constructs monotone dCRH from CRH; weakening the assumption to dCRH remains a distinct open target.
solved_when: A construction of monotone dCRH is given whose sole assumption is ordinary dCRH (rather than CRH).
why: It would clarify the minimum negation complexity required for cryptographic hardness.
key_works: Puniamurthy (2026), *A Note on the Existence of Monotone Distributional Collision Resistant Hash Functions*, IACR CiC 3(1), article 11.

title: Negation complexity of second-preimage resistance
subfield: Minimal assumptions, meta-complexity, and remaining post-quantum constructions
open: How much negation power must a hash family have to achieve second-preimage resistance — and does the answer coincide with what monotone distributional collision resistance requires? Formally, determine the tight negation requirements for second-preimage-resistant families and their relationship to monotone distributional collision resistance.
status: Existing monotonicity results distinguish OWFs, CRH, and dCRH rather than providing a complete classification. Puniamurthy (2026), *A Note on the Existence of Monotone Distributional Collision Resistant Hash Functions*, is the key work.
solved_when: A tight characterization of the negation complexity needed for second-preimage resistance is established, together with a precise account of its relationship to monotone distributional collision resistance (equivalence or separation).
why: It would expose structural differences between related hardness notions, clarifying which cryptographic primitives genuinely require non-monotone computation.
key_works: Puniamurthy (2026), *A Note on the Existence of Monotone Distributional Collision Resistant Hash Functions*.

title: Efficiently samplable pseudorandomness from worst-case meta-complexity
subfield: Minimal assumptions, meta-complexity, and remaining post-quantum constructions
open: Can the seed distributions arising in worst-case meta-complexity implications — which are currently nonconstructive or inefficiently samplable — be replaced by efficiently samplable ones under comparable assumptions? Put differently, can the conditional pseudorandomness these implications yield be upgraded to an ordinary, efficiently usable pseudorandom generator?
status: The 2026 implications of Liu–Mazor–Pass (ePrint 2026/668) carefully distinguish conditional pseudorandomness from an ordinary efficiently usable PRG, leaving the efficient-sampling question open.
solved_when: A worst-case meta-complexity hardness assumption comparable to the existing ones yields a pseudorandom generator whose output is efficiently samplable, rather than merely conditionally pseudorandom or nonconstructively specified.
why: It would move worst-case hardness from a purely structural phenomenon toward deployable cryptography, closing the gap between meta-complexity-based implications and practically usable pseudorandomness.
key_works: Liu–Mazor–Pass (2026), *Cryptographic Implications of Worst-Case Hardness of Time-Bounded Kolmogorov Complexity*, ePrint 2026/668.

bib.title: Efficiently samplable pseudorandomness from worst-case meta-complexity

title: Stronger zero knowledge from worst-case meta-complexity
subfield: Minimal assumptions, meta-complexity, and remaining post-quantum constructions
open: Can the known implications from worst-case hardness of meta-complexity problems (such as time-bounded Kolmogorov complexity) to zero knowledge be strengthened to hold without qualifications — that is, removing the bounded-auxiliary-input condition and the requirement of an inefficient prover?
status: The 2026 results (Liu–Mazor–Pass, *Cryptographic Implications of Worst-Case Hardness of Time-Bounded Kolmogorov Complexity*, ePrint 2026/668) establish only qualified forms of these implications, not every conventional efficient zero-knowledge guarantee.
solved_when: The worst-case meta-complexity zero-knowledge implications hold unconditionally in their standard form: for arbitrary (not just bounded) auxiliary inputs, with an efficient (polynomial-time) prover, yielding conventional efficient zero-knowledge guarantees.
why: It would firm up the bridge from worst-case complexity assumptions to cryptographic protocols, making meta-complexity hardness a cleaner and more usable foundation for zero knowledge.
key_works: Liu–Mazor–Pass (2026), *Cryptographic Implications of Worst-Case Hardness of Time-Bounded Kolmogorov Complexity*, ePrint 2026/668.

title: A natural concrete instance of genuine Microcrypt
subfield: Minimal assumptions, meta-complexity, and remaining post-quantum constructions
open: Does there exist a natural quantum cryptographic assumption that is plausibly weaker than classical one-way functions, together with evidence that it does not secretly imply them?
status: A 2026 Hamiltonian-phase-state analysis shows that one proposed route implies OWFs (Carrasco et al. (2026), *Instantiating Microcrypt: Obstacles and Opportunities via Tailored State Certification*, arXiv:2609.15842).
solved_when: A concrete, natural quantum assumption is identified and shown, with supporting evidence, not to imply classical one-way functions.
why: It would demonstrate a genuinely weaker quantum foundation for cryptography rather than hardness disguised as classical one-wayness.
key_works: Carrasco et al. (2026), *Instantiating Microcrypt: Obstacles and Opportunities via Tailored State Certification*, arXiv:2609.15842.

title: Multi-copy pseudorandom states from general quantum one-wayness
subfield: Minimal assumptions, meta-complexity, and remaining post-quantum constructions
open: Can reusable multi-copy pseudorandom states be constructed from any efficiently verifiable notion of quantum one-wayness, rather than from stronger or more structured assumptions? Non-black-box techniques are permitted.
status: Quantum one-wayness is known to lack the complete one-way-function-to-pseudorandom-generator equivalence available in the classical setting; see Cavalar–Goldin–Gray–Hall–Liu–Pelecanos (2025), *On the Computational Hardness of Quantum One-Wayness*, DOI: 10.22331/q-2025-03-27-1679.
solved_when: A construction is given that starts from general efficiently verifiable quantum one-wayness and yields reusable multi-copy pseudorandom states.
why: It would identify a minimal foundation for quantum pseudorandomness, playing the role that the classical OWF-to-PRG equivalence plays classically.
key_works: Cavalar–Goldin–Gray–Hall–Liu–Pelecanos (2025), *On the Computational Hardness of Quantum One-Wayness*, DOI: 10.22331/q-2025-03-27-1679.

title: The copy threshold for unconditional quantum one-wayness
subfield: Minimal assumptions, meta-complexity, and remaining post-quantum constructions
open: Where exactly does information-theoretic quantum one-wayness give way to computational hardness as the number of copies an adversary receives grows? Formally, determine the copy threshold at which functions that are one-way against copy-bounded adversaries cease to be one-way unconditionally and computational assumptions become necessary.
status: Both unconditional and computational regimes are known, but they leave open a quantitative threshold rather than settling a simple yes/no equivalence; see Cavalar et al. (2025), *On the Computational Hardness of Quantum One-Wayness*, DOI: 10.22331/q-2025-03-27-1679. Related tools include quantum tomography and sample-complexity thresholds.
solved_when: A quantitative copy threshold is identified — a precise number of copies (or sample-complexity bound) separating the unconditional regime from the regime requiring computational hardness, with matching positive and negative results.
why: It would pinpoint the exact moment quantum cryptography shifts from unconditional security to computational assumptions, sharpening the boundary traced by known hardness results for quantum one-wayness.
key_works: Cavalar et al. (2025), *On the Computational Hardness of Quantum One-Wayness*, DOI: 10.22331/q-2025-03-27-1679.

title: Many-time QCCC signatures from minimal puzzles
subfield: Minimal assumptions, meta-complexity, and remaining post-quantum constructions
open: What is the weakest puzzle assumption that suffices for building many-time secure signatures in the QCCC model, where computation is quantum but communication is classical? More precisely, characterize the minimal puzzle complexity needed for reusable (many-time) signature schemes in this setting.
status: Recent work by Chen–Wang–Xie (2026), *The Breakdown of Classical Minicrypt Equivalences in the Quantum-Computation Classical-Communication Model* (arXiv:2609.33098), established one-time equivalences and oracle separations, but these do not establish the corresponding many-time hierarchy.
solved_when: A many-time signature scheme in the QCCC model is constructed from a puzzle assumption strictly weaker than previously used, or a matching impossibility/oracle separation shows no weaker puzzle assumption can suffice — thereby establishing the many-time hierarchy analogous to the known one-time picture.
why: Without a many-time (reusable) signature scheme, authentication in the QCCC model remains a one-shot primitive, which is too weak for meaningful cryptographic systems; settling the minimal assumption determines the true foundation of post-quantum authentication.
key_works: Chen–Wang–Xie (2026), *The Breakdown of Classical Minicrypt Equivalences in the Quantum-Computation Classical-Communication Model*, arXiv:2609.33098.

bib.title: Many-time QCCC signatures from minimal puzzles

title: QCCC commitments from general efficiently verifiable puzzles
subfield: Minimal assumptions, meta-complexity, and remaining post-quantum constructions
open: Can quantum-commitment-to-classical-strings (QCCC) schemes be built from arbitrary efficiently verifiable puzzles, without any extra distributional assumption on the puzzle instances — or are such distributional restrictions provably necessary?
status: Recent positive results and oracle separations distinguish puzzle variants; they do not yield a blanket equivalence (Chen–Wang–Xie (2026), arXiv:2609.33098).
solved_when: Either a construction of QCCC commitments from general efficiently verifiable puzzles (no distributional restrictions) is given, or a proof that some distributional restriction is necessary for any such construction.
why: Commitments are a gateway primitive: obtaining them from minimal puzzle assumptions would unlock richer quantum-classical protocols and clarify the minimal post-quantum assumptions needed.
key_works: Chen–Wang–Xie (2026), arXiv:2609.33098.

title: Tests of noncommutativity from weaker assumptions
subfield: Minimal assumptions, meta-complexity, and remaining post-quantum constructions
open: Can we construct useful classical tests that certify noncommuting quantum observables, starting from weaker cryptographic assumptions such as suitable oblivious transfer, rather than from specialized trapdoor-claw-free structure?
status: The 2026 work of Bartusek–Shalit (*On the Cryptographic Structure Required for Verifying Qubits*, ePrint 2026/1215) establishes strong cryptographic consequences of such tests, sharpening the construction question.
solved_when: A classical test for noncommuting observables is constructed and proved sound from a weaker assumption (e.g., suitable OT), with no reliance on trapdoor-claw-free structure.
why: It would weaken the assumptions needed for the classical certification of quantum behavior, broadening the cryptographic foundations of quantum verification.
key_works: Bartusek–Shalit (2026), *On the Cryptographic Structure Required for Verifying Qubits*, ePrint 2026/1215.

title: Efficient LWE-based verifiable delay
subfield: Minimal assumptions, meta-complexity, and remaining post-quantum constructions
open: Can a useful verifiable delay function be built on an ordinary lattice foundation such as LWE? A satisfactory construction would come from a clearly specified lattice-based hardness assumption, separate the ordinary hardness argument from the claimed inherent sequentiality, and keep verification inexpensive.
status: Current post-quantum VDF research includes isogeny-based routes, notably Chávez-Saab–Rodríguez-Henríquez–Tibouchi (2021/2022), *Verifiable Isogeny Walks: Towards an Isogeny-Based Postquantum VDF*, DOI: 10.1007/978-3-030-99277-4_21; however, this does not settle the question of an ordinary-lattice foundation or of optimal verification.
solved_when: A VDF is constructed and proven sound from a clearly specified lattice-based assumption, with the security argument for the underlying hardness kept distinct from the sequentiality argument, and with verification cost low enough to qualify as inexpensive.
why: It would diversify delay-based cryptography beyond specialized algebraic platforms such as isogenies, giving post-quantum delay primitives a foundation that does not depend on those structures.
key_works: Chávez-Saab–Rodríguez-Henríquez–Tibouchi (2021/2022), *Verifiable Isogeny Walks: Towards an Isogeny-Based Postquantum VDF*, DOI: 10.1007/978-3-030-99277-4_21.
