title: A proof-aware open-problem registry
subfield: Data, infrastructure, validation, and funding gaps
open: Can we build a registry of open cryptographic problems that is machine-readable and proof-aware — recording assumptions, security interfaces, parameter regimes, reductions, counterexamples, and solved-by relationships — such that it automatically retires refuted conjectures while preserving valid nearby repair problems?
status: No full registry yet exists; the key validation point identified is a decisive acceptance test — retiring refuted conjectures while preserving valid nearby repair problems. A concrete refutation case is available: Jin (2026), *Low-Norm Nullstellensatz Hypothesis for the AND Code is False*, ePrint 2026/1087. Related infrastructure includes theorem-dependency graphs and machine-checked mathematics.
solved_when: A maintained registry exists that encodes assumptions, security interfaces, parameter regimes, reductions, counterexamples, and solved-by relationships for cryptographic problems, and demonstrably retires refuted conjectures while preserving valid nearby repair problems (e.g., the refutation of the low-norm Nullstellensatz hypothesis for the AND code does not delete legitimate adjacent open questions).
why: Stale assumptions can contaminate an entire census: a registry that cannot distinguish refuted from merely weakened problems propagates false premises into downstream research prioritization and funding.
key_works: Jin (2026), *Low-Norm Nullstellensatz Hypothesis for the AND Code is False*, ePrint 2026/1087.

title: An executable cryptanalysis corpus
subfield: Data, infrastructure, validation, and funding gaps
open: Can the community maintain a living, executable corpus of cryptanalytic attacks — starting with the attacks on witness encryption and graded encoding schemes — packaged with vulnerable interfaces, concrete parameters, expected outputs, and the code modifications that survive known defenses?
status: Papers document these attacks — notably Jo (2026), *Cryptanalysis of a Candidate Witness Encryption Scheme for Affine Determinant Programs*, ePrint 2026/1583 — but no maintained cross-construction regression corpus currently exists; such a corpus is regarded as a stronger infrastructure target than scattered documentation.
solved_when: The corpus exists as maintained infrastructure containing executable attack artifacts for witness encryption and graded encoding constructions, each with its vulnerable interface, parameters, expected outputs, and surviving modifications, and it serves as a cross-construction regression suite that is kept up to date.
why: Executable attack records would make rediscovery unnecessary and stop broken or partially repaired variants of these schemes from re-entering circulation unnoticed.
key_works: Jo (2026), *Cryptanalysis of a Candidate Witness Encryption Scheme for Affine Determinant Programs*, ePrint 2026/1583.

title: Whole-stack post-quantum proof auditing
subfield: Data, infrastructure, validation, and funding gaps
open: Can we build tooling that automatically audits an entire proof stack — every reduction, commitment, hash model, extractor, recursive wrapper, and setup assumption — and verifies that each component remains valid against quantum adversaries?
status: The current state of the art recognizes that quantum-hard underlying problems are necessary but insufficient: the reduction itself must support quantum adversaries. Attema et al. (2026), *A Survey on Security Reductions in Post-Quantum Cryptography*, ePrint 2026/846, surveys this landscape; related directions include proof-assistant automation and compositional security verification.
solved_when: A working automated system exists that tracks quantum-validity across all components of a proof stack (reductions, commitments, hash models, extractors, recursive wrappers, and setup assumptions), flagging any classical-only element.
why: A single classical-only component can invalidate an otherwise post-quantum design, so whole-stack verification is what ultimately determines whether a scheme is truly quantum-safe.
key_works: Attema et al. (2026), *A Survey on Security Reductions in Post-Quantum Cryptography*, ePrint 2026/846.

title: Advantage–time-aware post-quantum security estimators
subfield: Data, infrastructure, validation, and funding gaps
open: Can we build post-quantum security estimators that track the full advantage–time trade-off curve of an attack as it passes through a reduction, rather than collapsing everything to a single bit-security figure? Formally, such a tool would take a concrete reduction and adversary resource parameters and propagate the entire advantage-as-a-function-of-time curve through it.
status: The 2026 survey (Attema et al. (2026), *A Survey on Security Reductions in Post-Quantum Cryptography*, ePrint 2026/846) explains how bit-security summaries can obscure meaningful differences between reductions, but no such estimator has been built.
solved_when: A usable estimator exists that, given a reduction and attack parameters, outputs the propagated advantage–time curve rather than a single bit-security number.
why: It would support less conservative but more defensible concrete parameter choices, since bit-security summaries can hide meaningful differences between reductions.
key_works: Attema et al. (2026), *A Survey on Security Reductions in Post-Quantum Cryptography*, ePrint 2026/846.

title: Complete-cost interoperable FHE benchmarks
subfield: Data, infrastructure, validation, and funding gaps
open: Can we establish interoperable benchmarks for fully homomorphic encryption that place competing implementations on a single, common footing — holding security estimates, precision, failure probability, key sizes, memory, energy, and plaintext baselines fixed across comparisons?
status: Existing implementations and benchmark efforts do not make isolated performance claims directly comparable.
solved_when: A benchmark suite exists under which implementations are compared under common security estimates, precision, failure probability, key sizes, memory, energy, and plaintext baselines, rendering performance claims directly comparable.
why: It would make claimed efficiency improvements falsifiable and reproducible, replacing isolated performance numbers with comparable evaluations.
key_works: Brandão–Peralta (2026), *NIST First Call for Multi-Party Threshold Schemes*, NISTIR 8214C, DOI: 10.6028/NIST.IR.8214C.

title: Quantum cryptographic resource benchmark suites
subfield: Data, infrastructure, validation, and funding gaps
open: Can we build a common benchmark suite that scores candidate constructions of quantum obfuscation, copy-protection, and quantum money on physical cost? The suite would measure each candidate in logical qubits, non-Clifford gates, memory duration, and tolerated physical error, so that different quantum cryptographic capabilities can be compared side by side.
status: Asymptotic construction papers — e.g., Huang–Tang (2026), *Obfuscation of Arbitrary Quantum Circuits*, arXiv:2601.08969 — do not define a common physical-cost benchmark.
solved_when: A published benchmark suite exists that assigns quantitative scores in logical qubits, non-Clifford gates, memory duration, and tolerated physical error for complete quantum-obfuscation, copy-protection, and money tasks, and different constructions' capabilities are operationally comparable under it.
why: It would make different quantum cryptographic capabilities operationally comparable, which is impossible today.
key_works: Huang–Tang (2026), *Obfuscation of Arbitrary Quantum Circuits*, arXiv:2601.08969.

title: Threshold-cryptography conformance across security models
subfield: Data, infrastructure, validation, and funding gaps
open: Can we build an executable conformance test suite that tells apart the distinct security guarantees a threshold-cryptography implementation may claim — passive versus malicious adversaries, adaptive corruptions, aborting versus robust behavior, and synchronous versus asynchronous networks — so that a failing or missing test pinpoints which guarantee is actually delivered?
status: NIST's 2026 call (Brandão–Peralta (2026), *NIST First Call for Multi-Party Threshold Schemes*, NISTIR 8214C) requests specifications, reference implementations, and experimental reports; shared adversarial conformance infrastructure remains a concrete target.
solved_when: A publicly available conformance-testing infrastructure exists that executes tests distinguishing passive, malicious, adaptive, aborting, robust, synchronous, and asynchronous guarantees, aligning with the specifications, reference implementations, and experimental reports requested by NIST's 2026 call.
why: Without such tests, interoperability efforts can silently weaken the intended security model — an implementation tuned for passive-adversary testing may pass while offering none of the malicious-security or robustness guarantees its deployment assumes.
key_works: Brandão–Peralta (2026), *NIST First Call for Multi-Party Threshold Schemes*, NISTIR 8214C.

title: Leakage-labeled benchmark datasets for encrypted computation
subfield: Data, infrastructure, validation, and funding gaps
open: Can the community publish benchmark workloads for encrypted computation that carry an explicit contract — permitted leakage, numerical tolerances, adversarial inputs, and utility requirements — instead of bare circuit files?
status: Current benchmarks typically ship circuit files alone, without the accompanying contract; the gap is articulated in Brandão–Peralta (2026) and NISTIR 8214C, with related concerns raised by Li–Micciancio (2020/2021), ePrint 2020/1533.
solved_when: Publicly available benchmark datasets exist in which each workload is labeled with its permitted leakage, numerical tolerances, adversarial inputs, and utility requirements.
why: Without the privacy and correctness contract attached to a benchmark, apparent speedups can be obtained by quietly changing the problem, rewarding incomparable or weakened functionality.
key_works: Brandão–Peralta (2026), NISTIR 8214C; Li–Micciancio (2020/2021), ePrint 2020/1533.

title: Upfront support alongside outcome-based research prizes
subfield: Data, infrastructure, validation, and funding gaps
open: Can a funding structure be established that pairs transparent upfront grants or fellowships with outcome-based prizes for clearly specified coding-theory challenges, so that researchers are supported before, not only after, a result?
status: The Proximity Prize offers a $1 million prize pool but explicitly states that it cannot award grants (official challenge rules and FAQ, checked October 2026), so no complementary upfront-support mechanism currently exists alongside it.
solved_when: A transparent upfront grant or fellowship program exists for clearly specified coding-theory challenges, complementing post-result rewards such as the Proximity Prize's $1 million prize pool.
why: Without upfront runway, researchers outside well-funded institutions may be unable to pursue the work at all, however substantial the eventual prize.
key_works: Proximity Prize, official challenge rules and FAQ, checked October 2026.

title: Sustained support for negative results and maintenance
subfield: Data, infrastructure, validation, and funding gaps
open: How can we sustainably fund the unglamorous work that keeps cryptographic claims trustworthy — independent cryptanalysis, archives of failed replications, tracking of assumption versions, and long-term maintenance of research artifacts — rather than rewarding only one-time constructions?
status: This is an incentive-design proposal, not a claim that no such funding exists; no comprehensive funding census was established here.
solved_when: A sustained funding mechanism (or dedicated program) exists that supports independent cryptanalysis, failed-replication archives, assumption-version tracking, and long-term maintenance of research artifacts on an ongoing basis, rather than as one-time construction rewards.
why: A one-time construction reward does not maintain the evidence needed to keep that construction trustworthy; without sustained support, the validation infrastructure underlying cryptographic confidence decays.

title: Bit-efficient Reed–Solomon decoding near capacity
subfield: Coding theory and practical transparent post-quantum proofs
open: Can Reed–Solomon codes be list-decoded (and proximity-tested) up to the near-capacity radii achieved over large alphabets by algorithms whose running time is polynomial in the block length \(n\) and \(\log q\), rather than in the field size \(q\) itself?
status: A September 2026 preprint (Jeronimo, *Algorithmic List Decoding at Capacity and Optimal Proximity Gaps for Reed–Solomon Codes*, arXiv:2609.05870) reports fixed-slack prime-field decoding with \(q^{O_\gamma(1)}\) running time.
solved_when: Near-capacity decoding guarantees matching the known large-alphabet results are achieved by an algorithm running in time polynomial in \(n\) and \(\log q\) (bit-efficient, no polynomial-in-\(q\) dependence).
why: Polynomial-in-\(q\) running times are unusable for cryptographic implementation, since the large fields required for capacity-approaching parameters make the algorithms impractical; bit-efficient decoding would make these codes viable for transparent post-quantum proof systems.
key_works: Jeronimo (2026), *Algorithmic List Decoding at Capacity and Optimal Proximity Gaps for Reed–Solomon Codes*, arXiv:2609.05870.

title: Unbounded-collusion bit-fixing CPRFs from OWFs
subfield: Constrained pseudorandom functions
open: Support arbitrarily many polynomially bounded colluding bit-fixing keys from OWFs alone.
status: Adaptive constant-collusion constructions exist; removing the collusion bound remains the target.
why: Bit-fixing is a basic family for access control and selective pseudorandomness.
key_works: Davidson–Katsumata–Nishimaki–Yamada (2018/2020), *Constrained PRFs for Bit-fixing (and More) from OWFs with Adaptive Security and Constant Collusion Resistance*, ePrint 2018/982.

title: General one-key private CPRFs from OWFs
subfield: Constrained pseudorandom functions
open: Can one construct constrained pseudorandom functions supporting arbitrary circuit constraints and privacy, in even the single-key setting, assuming only the existence of one-way functions? Formally: build one-key private constrained PRFs for all circuits from any OWF.
status: The 2026 black-box separation from key agreement by Bi–Ma–Dai (2026), *Limits on the Power of Private Constrained PRFs*, DOI: 10.4230/LIPIcs.ITC.2026.2, does not supply a construction from OWFs, leaving the problem open.
solved_when: An explicit construction of one-key private constrained PRFs for all circuits is given, proved secure under the sole assumption that one-way functions exist.
why: It would isolate a genuinely useful private-programming capability that sits strictly below public-key cryptography in assumptions.
key_works: Bi–Ma–Dai (2026), *Limits on the Power of Private Constrained PRFs*, DOI: 10.4230/LIPIcs.ITC.2026.2.

title: Non-black-box key agreement from private CPRFs
subfield: Constrained pseudorandom functions
open: Do general one-key private constrained PRFs imply key agreement once we allow non-black-box techniques? Formally, is there a non-black-box construction of key agreement from any private CPRF family supporting a single key constraint?
status: Recent work by Bi–Ma–Dai (2026), *Limits on the Power of Private Constrained PRFs* (DOI: 10.4230/LIPIcs.ITC.2026.2), excludes specified black-box constructions but does not rule out unrestricted, non-black-box implications.
solved_when: A proof (via any non-black-box method) that one-key private CPRFs imply key agreement, or a proof that no such implication exists; the question is resolved in either direction.
why: A solution would pin down where private CPRFs sit in the Minicrypt-versus-Cryptomania assumption hierarchy, telling us whether these objects are inherently public-key.
key_works: Bi–Ma–Dai (2026), *Limits on the Power of Private Constrained PRFs*, DOI: 10.4230/LIPIcs.ITC.2026.2.

title: Tight constrained-key size lower bounds
subfield: Constrained pseudorandom functions
open: Can we characterize, for constrained pseudorandom functions, exactly how large constrained keys must be as a function of predicate complexity, permitted leakage, and collusion count — matching the known upper bounds with corresponding lower bounds? A complete quantitative classification would pin down which capability-description costs are information-theoretically unavoidable.
status: Existing family-specific constructions and separations do not give a complete quantitative classification.
solved_when: For each family of constraints, proven lower bounds on constrained-key size match the best constructions (as functions of predicate complexity, permitted leakage, and collusion count) up to constant factors, closing all gaps.
why: It would separate unavoidable capability-description costs from merely inefficient constructions, telling us which existing schemes are optimal and where fundamentally better designs are possible.
key_works: Langrehr (2025/2026), ePrint 2025/1338; Davidson et al. (2018/2020), ePrint 2018/982.

title: xiO from plain LWE
subfield: Exponentially efficient, decomposable, and succinct obfuscation
open: Can we build xiO — obfuscation with exponential efficiency, decomposability, and succinctness — whose security rests on ordinary LWE alone, with no equivocation, evasiveness, or specialized circular assumptions? More precisely, is there a nontrivially compressing xiO from plain LWE?
status: New lattice obfuscation routes have not removed all additional assumptions, even when compression itself is used as an intermediate goal; related directions include succinct randomized encodings and time–space tradeoffs (Lin et al., 2016, ePrint 2016/006; Cini–Lai–Woo, 2025, ePrint 2025/1129).
solved_when: A construction of xiO achieving nontrivial compression is given, with a security proof from standard LWE, without relying on equivocal, evasive, or specialized circular assumptions.
why: xiO from plain LWE would be a potentially more accessible milestone on the path to polynomial-time indistinguishability obfuscation, whose security assumptions are far better understood than the specialized ones currently needed.
key_works: Lin et al. (2016), ePrint 2016/006; Cini–Lai–Woo (2025), ePrint 2025/1129.

title: Fully succinct unrestricted obfuscation without additional helpers
subfield: Exponentially efficient, decomposable, and succinct obfuscation
open: Can we build obfuscation that is fully succinct in its input length — with no separate helper assumptions — starting only from polynomially hard circuit indistinguishability obfuscation? Formally, the goal is unrestricted, fully input-succinct obfuscation without additionally assuming succinct witness encryption or suitable unique-proof succinct arguments.
status: Recent proof-restricted constructions identify additional ingredients needed to achieve stronger succinctness; see Jain–Jin–Mathialagan–Paneth (2025/2026), *On Succinct Obfuscation via Propositional Proofs*, ePrint 2026/2009.
solved_when: A construction of fully input-succinct unrestricted obfuscation is given, basing security solely on polynomially hard circuit iO, with no separate reliance on succinct witness encryption or unique-proof succinct arguments.
why: It would make the size of an obfuscated secret program largely independent of the eventual bound on the input length it must handle.
key_works: Jain–Jin–Mathialagan–Paneth (2025/2026), *On Succinct Obfuscation via Propositional Proofs*, ePrint 2026/2009.

title: Boolean FHE within 10× native latency
subfield: FHE rate, native cost, numerical correctness, and implementation
open: Can fully homomorphic encryption become practical enough that an entire Boolean workload runs within 10× the latency of the same computation on plaintext — counting every refresh and preprocessing cost that real deployment requires?
status: Specialized FHE processor instructions already exist — notably the PulpFHE complex instruction set extensions of Ahmed–Tsoutsos (2024), ePrint 2024/1315 — but these are components; the 10× figure is an end-to-end target, not a claimed universal record. Related efforts include circuit-depth optimization and accelerator architecture.
solved_when: A broad, pre-declared suite of Boolean workloads is evaluated end-to-end under FHE within 10× matched plaintext latency, with refresh and amortized preprocessing included in the accounting.
why: Meeting this bound would fundamentally change the economics of confidential computation, making encrypted outsourcing competitive for realistic workloads rather than a niche of extreme overhead.
key_works: Ahmed–Tsoutsos (2024), *PulpFHE: Complex Instruction Set Extensions for FHE Processors*, ePrint 2024/1315.

title: Matrix FHE within 10× native matrix computation
subfield: FHE rate, native cost, numerical correctness, and implementation
open: Can a fully homomorphic encryption scheme execute complete encrypted matrix workloads end to end within 10× the cost of a matched plaintext run, once every overhead — data movement, key management, and bootstrapping — is counted? The target is near-native performance for matrix computation under encryption, not just fast isolated components.
status: Matrix-native bootstrapping improves specific components, but it does not establish near-native end-to-end execution. Shokri–Tsoutsos (2026), *Low-Depth Bootstrapping for Matrix-Native FHE*, ePrint 2026/811, is the key work.
solved_when: An FHE system executes full encrypted matrix workloads within 10× the runtime of an equivalent plaintext execution on matched hardware, with the accounting including data movement, key operations, and bootstrapping.
why: Matrix computation underlies many high-value private workloads; bringing encrypted execution within a small constant factor of plaintext would make privacy-preserving versions of these workloads practical.
key_works: Shokri–Tsoutsos (2026), *Low-Depth Bootstrapping for Matrix-Native FHE*, ePrint 2026/811.

title: Post-quantum verification below 10% of FHE evaluation cost
subfield: FHE rate, native cost, numerical correctness, and implementation
open: Can a fully homomorphic encryption evaluation be accompanied by a post-quantum, transparently checkable proof that the computation was carried out correctly, at a cost below 10% of the evaluation itself?
status: PRISM (Zhou–Li–Yang–Hong–Wei, 2026, *PRISM: Efficient zkSNARKs for RNS-Based Homomorphic Encryption*, ePrint 2026/1956) advances practical verification of standard RNS-based homomorphic encryption, but the stated low-overhead post-quantum target remains stronger than what is currently achieved.
solved_when: A verification scheme exists whose post-quantum argument adds less than 10% overhead to a declared FHE evaluation workload, with correctness of the evaluation verifiable by any party without trusting the evaluator.
why: Confidential computation should not require trusting the evaluator's answer; verifiable FHE would let outsourced computation remain private yet auditable by the client.
key_works: Zhou–Li–Yang–Hong–Wei (2026), *PRISM: Efficient zkSNARKs for RNS-Based Homomorphic Encryption*, ePrint 2026/1956.

title: Removing circularity from lattice-isomorphism FHE
subfield: Fully homomorphic encryption: construction foundations
open: Can fully homomorphic encryption supporting unbounded-depth evaluation be built from an ordinary lattice-isomorphism assumption alone? Equivalently, obtain unrestricted-depth FHE in this setting without assuming circular security as an additional hypothesis.
status: Recent work supplies FHE from lattice isomorphism under a circular-security assumption, together with separate leveled constructions (Branco–Malavolta–Maradni 2025, ePrint 2025/993; Bennett–Lai–Stephens-Davidowitz 2026, *Advanced Cryptography from Lattice Isomorphism—New Constructions of IBE and FHE*, ePrint 2026/465).
solved_when: A construction of unrestricted-depth FHE is given whose security reduces to a standard lattice-isomorphism assumption, with no separate circular-security assumption invoked.
why: It would firm up a newly emerging foundation for homomorphic encryption on lattice-isomorphism problems, removing the need to assume circular security on top of it.
key_works: Branco–Malavolta–Maradni (2025), ePrint 2025/993; Bennett–Lai–Stephens-Davidowitz (2026), *Advanced Cryptography from Lattice Isomorphism—New Constructions of IBE and FHE*, ePrint 2026/465.

title: Genuinely refresh-free unrestricted FHE
subfield: Fully homomorphic encryption: construction foundations
open: Can we build fully homomorphic encryption that supports arbitrary polynomial-depth computation from fixed parameters, while avoiding any refresh mechanism — no bootstrapping via homomorphic decryption, no encrypted-secret-key refresh material, and no disguised operation playing the same role? A second sentence sharpens this: the scheme should be "leveled-free yet unbounded," achieving genuine unrestricted depth with parameters independent of the target circuit.
status: Current "without bootstrapping" constructions, in the lineage of Brakerski–Gentry–Vaikuntanathan (ePrint 2011/277), are leveled: they require a preset depth bound and thus do not meet this specification. The recent Fully-Homomorphic Encryption from Lattice Isomorphism of Branco–Malavolta–Maradni (2025, ePrint 2025/993) likewise does not satisfy the refresh-free unrestricted-depth requirement. No existing scheme achieves the stated goal.
solved_when: An explicit FHE construction is given that (i) uses fixed parameters not depending on the depth of the computation, (ii) supports arbitrary polynomial-depth circuits, and (iii) contains no homomorphic decryption step, no encrypted-secret-key refresh material, and no substituted operation serving the refresh role — with a proof of correctness and security.
why: It would remove the recurring maintenance operation from encrypted computation, eliminating the dominant cost and complexity bottleneck that refresh/bootstrapping imposes on every existing unbounded-depth FHE scheme.
key_works: Brakerski–Gentry–Vaikuntanathan, ePrint 2011/277; Branco–Malavolta–Maradni (2025), *Fully-Homomorphic Encryption from Lattice Isomorphism*, ePrint 2025/993.

title: FHE from arbitrary public-key encryption
subfield: Fully homomorphic encryption: construction foundations
open: Can fully homomorphic encryption be built from any public-key encryption scheme, if we allow arbitrary non-black-box use of the underlying scheme? In other words, is every public-key encryption scheme — no matter how unstructured — sufficient for compact FHE?
status: Known constructions use substantially more structure than arbitrary public-key encryption. Key works: Brakerski–Gentry–Vaikuntanathan, ePrint 2011/277; Bennett–Lai–Stephens-Davidowitz (2026), ePrint 2026/465.
solved_when: A construction of compact fully homomorphic encryption is given whose only assumption is the existence of public-key encryption, with unrestricted non-black-box access to the underlying scheme.
why: It determines whether homomorphic computation is a genuinely additional cryptographic foundation or a consequence of encryption itself.
key_works: Brakerski–Gentry–Vaikuntanathan, ePrint 2011/277; Bennett–Lai–Stephens-Davidowitz (2026), ePrint 2026/465.

title: Fully succinct unleveled multi-key FHE from plain LWE
subfield: Fully homomorphic encryption: construction foundations
open: Can one build a multi-key fully homomorphic encryption scheme that is fully succinct — with keys and ciphertexts whose size does not grow with the number of participants — and simultaneously supports unbounded (unleveled) computation depth, all under the plain Learning With Errors assumption?
status: The 2026 fully succinct result (Afshar–Goyal, *Fully-Succinct Multi-Key FHE & Rate-1 Simulatable Threshold Decryption from LWE*, ePrint 2026/1683) is leveled; achieving participant independence does not remove that qualification, so unrestricted depth remains out of reach.
solved_when: A multi-key FHE construction from plain LWE exists in which key and ciphertext sizes are independent of the number of participants (full succinctness) and the scheme supports unrestricted evaluation depth rather than being leveled.
why: It would unify the two major compactness goals of multi-key FHE — participant-count independence and depth independence — in a single construction, enabling dynamic distributed computation on encrypted data without re-encrypting or key management tied to the participant set.
key_works: Afshar–Goyal (2026), *Fully-Succinct Multi-Key FHE & Rate-1 Simulatable Threshold Decryption from LWE*, ePrint 2026/1683.

title: Function-hiding general FE from lattices
subfield: Functional encryption for general circuits
open: Can we construct functional encryption for general circuits, from plain lattice assumptions, that hides both the encrypted data and the program embedded in the functional key — beyond whatever the function's output inherently reveals? More precisely: is a function-hiding general-purpose FE scheme achievable under standard lattice assumptions without resorting to idealized models such as generic groups?
status: Existing constructions handle only restricted function families, and generic-group techniques yield barriers rather than solutions; neither settles function hiding for general circuits from lattices. Hajiabadi–Langrehr–Wang (2026), *Generic-Group Barriers for Function-Hiding and Multi-Input Functional Encryption*, ePrint 2026/1149, establish the generic-group barriers in this area.
solved_when: A functional encryption scheme for general circuits is given, based on plain lattice assumptions, in which the ciphertext conceals the encrypted data and the functional key conceals its function, up to unavoidable leakage of the function's output, with a proof of security under standard lattice assumptions.
why: Function hiding protects the key holder's proprietary models and queries, not just the input data, so both sides of the computation remain secret — something current general-circuit FE from lattices does not provide.
key_works: Hajiabadi–Langrehr–Wang (2026), *Generic-Group Barriers for Function-Hiding and Multi-Input Functional Encryption*, ePrint 2026/1149.

title: Strong randomized MIFE without subexponential iO
subfield: Functional encryption for general circuits
open: Can we build adaptive multi-input functional encryption for randomized functionalities, secure against both malicious encryptors and malicious decryptors, while relying only on polynomial-strength assumptions — in particular, without subexponentially secure indistinguishability obfuscation? Formally, the goal is a construction achieving the same security and functionality as the strongest known schemes, but replacing the subexponential iO building block.
status: The 2025 construction of Datta–Guan–Korb–Sahai (ePrint 2025/330) supports unbounded messages per slot and achieves security against malicious encryptors and decryptors, but relies on subexponential iO; that functionality itself is no longer open — the open question is removing the subexponential iO dependency.
solved_when: A construction is given for adaptive randomized multi-input FE with security against malicious encryptors and decryptors (and supporting unbounded messages per slot, as in the 2025 scheme) that requires no subexponentially secure iO.
why: Without such a construction, the randomness used in randomized functionalities remains a potential covert channel through which malicious encryptors or decryptors can leak secrets; a solution closes this gap using standard assumptions.
key_works: Datta–Guan–Korb–Sahai (2025), *(Multi-Input) FE for Randomized Functionalities, Revisited*, ePrint 2025/330.

title: Information-theoretic publicly verifiable secret-sharing deletion
subfield: Homomorphic secret sharing, garbling, and preprocessing
open: Can secret sharing be made deletable in a way anyone can verify, using only information-theoretic means? Formally, construct information-theoretic secret sharing with publicly verifiable deletion, where verification requires no secret information held by the participants.
status: The 2026 unanimously verifiable construction of Chen–Ji–Luo (*Linearly Homomorphic Secret Sharing and Multi-Party Computation with Unanimously Verifiable Deletion*, ePrint 2026/1673) explicitly leaves public verification as a stronger, open target.
solved_when: A construction of information-theoretic secret sharing is given in which deletion is publicly verifiable — any party, without secret verification information, can check that deletion occurred.
why: Today, verifying deletion requires unanimous agreement among the relevant participants holding secret verification information; public verification would let any external party audit deletion.
key_works: Chen–Ji–Luo (2026), *Linearly Homomorphic Secret Sharing and Multi-Party Computation with Unanimously Verifiable Deletion*, ePrint 2026/1673.

title: General-purpose iO from plain LWE
subfield: Indistinguishability obfuscation: foundational assumptions
open: Can we base indistinguishability obfuscation for all polynomial-size Boolean circuits on plain LWE alone? That is, an iO construction whose only assumption is ordinary polynomially hard LWE, with no evasive, circular, equivocal, pairing, or knowledge-type assumptions.
status: General iO currently has multi-assumption constructions; the 2025 lattice route still requires Equivocal LWE and NTRU-related machinery (Cini–Lai–Woo 2025, *Lattice-based Obfuscation from NTRU and Equivocal LWE*, ePrint 2025/1129), following earlier well-founded multi-assumption work of Jain–Lin–Sahai (2021, *Indistinguishability Obfuscation from Well-Founded Assumptions*, ePrint 2020/1003).
solved_when: A construction of iO for all polynomial-size Boolean circuits is proved secure under ordinary polynomially hard LWE alone, with no additional assumptions.
why: It would put general software obfuscation on a widely studied post-quantum foundation.
key_works: Jain–Lin–Sahai (2021), *Indistinguishability Obfuscation from Well-Founded Assumptions*, ePrint 2020/1003; Cini–Lai–Woo (2025), *Lattice-based Obfuscation from NTRU and Equivocal LWE*, ePrint 2025/1129.

title: General-purpose iO from one-way functions
subfield: Indistinguishability obfuscation: foundational assumptions
open: Can general-purpose indistinguishability obfuscation for circuits be constructed from the minimal assumption that one-way functions exist, if we allow genuinely non-black-box techniques in both the construction and the reduction?
status: Black-box limitations — as in Asharov–Segev (2015), *Limits on the Power of Indistinguishability Obfuscation and Functional Encryption*, ePrint 2015/341 — rule out black-box approaches, but they do not establish an unrestricted impossibility theorem, leaving the non-black-box route open.
solved_when: A construction of iO for all polynomial-size circuits is given, provably secure under arbitrary one-way functions alone, with no black-box restriction on the techniques used.
why: It would collapse the assumption base of the entire obfuscation-and-functional-encryption application ecosystem down to the most standard assumption in cryptography, clarifying whether iO sits in Minicrypt or requires structure above it.
key_works: Asharov–Segev (2015), *Limits on the Power of Indistinguishability Obfuscation and Functional Encryption*, ePrint 2015/341.

title: Unrestricted iO without subexponential hardness
subfield: Indistinguishability obfuscation: foundational assumptions
open: Can unrestricted circuit indistinguishability obfuscation be built from assumptions that are only polynomially hard and independently studied, so that security does not rely on subexponential hardness gained through complexity leveraging?
status: Current constructions achieving unrestricted iO, such as Jain–Lin–Sahai (2021, ePrint 2020/1003), do not avoid this barrier. Recent progress on polynomial hardness — e.g., Dujmovic–Hsieh–Jain–Quach (2026), *How to use Polynomially-Hard iO: Turing Machine Obfuscation and More*, ePrint 2026/1636 — applies to proof-restricted obfuscation and does not itself construct unrestricted iO from polynomially hard conventional assumptions.
solved_when: A construction of unrestricted iO for circuits is given, whose security reduces to polynomially hard, independently studied assumptions with no complexity leveraging step requiring subexponential security.
why: It would substantially reduce the gap between asymptotic existence results and meaningful concrete parameters, making iO plausible to instantiate in practice.
key_works: Jain–Lin–Sahai (2021), ePrint 2020/1003; Dujmovic–Hsieh–Jain–Quach (2026), *How to use Polynomially-Hard iO: Turing Machine Obfuscation and More*, ePrint 2026/1636.

title: Equivocal LWE from ordinary LWE
subfield: Indistinguishability obfuscation: foundational assumptions
open: Does Equivocal LWE follow from ordinary LWE, or is it genuinely a stronger assumption? A proof of reduction, or a separating attack, would settle the question.
status: Equivocal LWE was introduced as an additional assumption in the 2025 lattice-obfuscation construction (Cini–Lai–Woo, *Lattice-based Obfuscation from NTRU and Equivocal LWE*, ePrint 2025/1129); no reduction to ordinary LWE or separating attack is known.
solved_when: Either a reduction from Equivocal LWE to standard LWE is established, or an attack is exhibited that breaks Equivocal LWE while ordinary LWE remains secure, thereby separating the two assumptions.
why: It isolates a concrete dependency on one route toward plain-LWE indistinguishability obfuscation: if the assumptions are equivalent, the 2025 lattice-obfuscation construction rests on ordinary LWE alone; if not, the extra assumption is a real bottleneck.
key_works: Cini–Lai–Woo (2025), *Lattice-based Obfuscation from NTRU and Equivocal LWE*, ePrint 2025/1129.

title: OWFs from \(P\neq NP\)
subfield: Minimal assumptions, meta-complexity, and remaining post-quantum constructions
open: Can cryptographic one-way functions be derived from worst-case NP hardness alone, with no additional average-case assumption? Equivalently, does \(P \neq NP\) suffice to imply the existence of one-way functions?
status: Modern meta-complexity characterizations have sharpened the gap between worst-case and average-case hardness but have not removed it, so the derivation of one-way functions from \(P \neq NP\) remains open; see Liu–Pass (2020), *On One-Way Functions and Kolmogorov Complexity*, DOI: 10.1109/FOCS46700.2020.00118, and Liu–Pass (2026), DOI: 10.4230/LIPIcs.ITCS.2026.97.
solved_when: A proof (or refutation) that one-way functions exist if and only if \(P \neq NP\) — in particular, a construction of one-way functions assuming only worst-case NP hardness, with no auxiliary average-case hypothesis.
why: It would tie the most basic object in cryptography to the central conjecture of complexity theory, placing the foundations of cryptography on the same worst-case hardness that underlies all of NP-completeness.
key_works: Liu–Pass (2020), *On One-Way Functions and Kolmogorov Complexity*, DOI: 10.1109/FOCS46700.2020.00118; Liu–Pass (2026), DOI: 10.4230/LIPIcs.ITCS.2026.97.

title: QCCC commitments from general efficiently verifiable puzzles
subfield: Minimal assumptions, meta-complexity, and remaining post-quantum constructions
open: Can quantum-classical-classical (QCCC) commitments be built from any efficiently verifiable puzzle, without imposing extra distributional assumptions on the puzzle? Alternatively, show that some such restriction is genuinely necessary.
status: Recent positive results and oracle separations distinguish puzzle variants, but they do not yield a blanket equivalence; the current constructions still carry distributional restrictions (Chen–Wang–Xie, 2026, arXiv:2609.33098).
solved_when: Either a construction of QCCC commitments from arbitrary efficiently verifiable puzzles is given, or a proof (e.g., via separation) demonstrates that distributional restrictions cannot be removed.
why: Commitments serve as a gateway primitive to richer quantum-classical protocols; settling this determines exactly how weak a puzzle assumption suffices, sharpening the minimal assumptions landscape for post-quantum cryptography.

title: Ciphertext-policy secret-key ABE for Turing machines
subfield: Restricted FE, attribute-based encryption, and registration
open: Can we build a ciphertext-policy version of secret-key attribute-based encryption supporting Turing-machine access policies, given that the key-policy version is known under circular small-secret LWE? In other words, obtain the dual construction in which the policy is attached to the ciphertext rather than to the key.
status: The September 2026 revision of Agrawal et al. (2026), *ABE for Unbounded Circuits from Circular LWE and Pairings* (ePrint 2026/1439), explicitly leaves the corresponding ciphertext-policy dual variants open.
solved_when: A secret-key ABE scheme for Turing machines with ciphertext-policy access structure is constructed (and proven secure) under circular small-secret LWE.
why: Policy placement determines who can express and update access rules, so the ciphertext-policy dual would shift control of access rules from the key issuer to the encryptor.
key_works: Agrawal et al. (2026), *ABE for Unbounded Circuits from Circular LWE and Pairings*, ePrint 2026/1439.

title: Tensor-preimage-hint security from ordinary LWE
subfield: Restricted FE, attribute-based encryption, and registration
open: Can the higher-degree tensor-preimage-hint assumption underlying polynomial functional encryption be justified on the standard hardness of LWE, or does an attack separate it from LWE? A resolution either takes the form of a reduction from ordinary LWE to the assumption, or a concrete attack showing the assumption is strictly weaker.
status: The 2026 construction of Cini–Lai–Ünal–Woo (*Lattice-based Secret-Key Functional Encryption for Constant-Degree Polynomials*, ePrint 2026/1977) reduces the degree-one case to LWE; higher degrees currently require a new assumption.
solved_when: Either a reduction from ordinary LWE to the higher-degree tensor-preimage-hint assumption is given, or a separating attack against the assumption (that LWE itself withstands) is exhibited.
why: It would establish a standard-assumption foundation for useful low-degree functional encryption, replacing a new, untested assumption with the well-studied LWE problem.
key_works: Cini–Lai–Ünal–Woo (2026), *Lattice-based Secret-Key Functional Encryption for Constant-Degree Polynomials*, ePrint 2026/1977.

title: Fully tight lattice inner-product FE
subfield: Restricted FE, attribute-based encryption, and registration
open: Can we construct a lattice-based inner-product functional encryption scheme whose security reduction is fully tight — losing nothing in the number of users or keys — while keeping ciphertexts and keys compact and adaptive security intact? More precisely, can the remaining slack in existing almost-tight reductions be eliminated?
status: The 2025 result of Han–Yi–Liu–Gu (*Tightly Secure Inner-Product Functional Encryption Revisited: Compact, Lattice-based, and More*, ePrint 2025/1613) gives an almost-tight LWE-based construction, but not a fully tight one; residual reduction losses remain.
solved_when: A lattice IPFE scheme is given whose reduction to LWE is fully tight (no loss in user count or key count, matching the almost-tight 2025 construction's compactness and adaptive security guarantees).
why: Tightness materially reduces the deployment parameters — and hence efficiency and cost — for systems serving many users and issuing many keys.
key_works: Han–Yi–Liu–Gu (2025), *Tightly Secure Inner-Product Functional Encryption Revisited: Compact, Lattice-based, and More*, ePrint 2025/1613.

title: Public-key two-sided attribute-hiding predicate encryption
subfield: Restricted FE, attribute-based encryption, and registration
open: Can the recent lattice-based two-sided attribute-hiding predicate encryption scheme be lifted from the symmetric-key setting to the public-key setting?
status: The lattice two-sided attribute-hiding approach exists in the symmetric-key setting (Cheng–Goyal 2026, *Collusion-Resistant Constrained PRFs for Compute-&-Compare Predicates from LWE*, ePrint 2026/1874, §2.5), where the public-key extension is explicitly left open.
solved_when: A public-key predicate encryption scheme, built from the lattice approach of Cheng–Goyal, achieves two-sided attribute hiding (both the encrypted attributes and the predicate are hidden) with collusion resistance as in the symmetric-key construction.
why: In the public-key setting anyone can encrypt without holding a shared encryption secret and without exposing the attributes or the predicate being tested.
key_works: Cheng–Goyal (2026), *Collusion-Resistant Constrained PRFs for Compute-&-Compare Predicates from LWE*, ePrint 2026/1874, §2.5.

title: Fully unbounded public-key ABE from plain LWE
subfield: Restricted FE, attribute-based encryption, and registration
open: Can public-key attribute-based encryption for general policies be built from plain LWE while allowing policies of unbounded depth and width? Formally, the goal is an ABE supporting circuits with neither a depth nor a width bound, under ordinary LWE alone — no pairings, circular-security assumptions, or obfuscation helper.
status: Current candidate constructions rely on stronger assumptions than plain LWE, and existing depth-unbounded, bounded-space results occupy a different parameter regime. Key works include Agrawal et al. (2026), ePrint 2026/1439, and Abram–Malavolta–Roy (2026), *Tree Encodings IV: Depth-Unbounded Attribute-Based Encryption and Delay Encryption*, ePrint 2026/2094.
solved_when: A public-key ABE from standard LWE supports arbitrary (unbounded-depth, unbounded-width) circuits as policies, with no stronger assumption or external primitive; the natural criterion for this construction target is a proof of security and correctness in this unbounded regime.
why: Encryption would no longer require fixing a prior bound on policy computation, removing the setup-time guess of how complex future policies may be.
key_works: Agrawal et al. (2026), ePrint 2026/1439; Abram–Malavolta–Roy (2026), *Tree Encodings IV: Depth-Unbounded Attribute-Based Encryption and Delay Encryption*, ePrint 2026/2094.

title: Almost-everywhere soundness for non-black-box LWE SNARKs
subfield: SNARG and SNARK foundations
open: Can the LWE-based SNARK of Jin–Lu–Peng (2026) be proved sound for all sufficiently large security parameters, rather than only along an infinite subsequence? Formally, replace infinitely-often soundness with eventual (almost-everywhere) soundness in the non-black-box reduction.
status: The current state of the art is the 2026 theorem of Jin–Lu–Peng, *SNARKs from LWE via Non-black-Box Reductions* (DOI: 10.1145/3798129.3800888), which achieves only infinitely-often security — a substantive limitation. The distinction between infinitely-often and eventual hardness is the known relevant framing.
solved_when: The construction of Jin–Lu–Peng (2026) is shown sound at all sufficiently large parameters — i.e., the non-black-box LWE reduction establishes soundness for every security parameter above some explicit bound, not merely for infinitely many.
why: Infinitely-often security means deployments can land on parameters where the proof gives no guarantee; almost-everywhere soundness would make the theorem usable at the parameters actually selected in practice.
key_works: Jin–Lu–Peng (2026), *SNARKs from LWE via Non-black-Box Reductions*, DOI: 10.1145/3798129.3800888.

title: Fully adaptive NP SNARGs from plain LWE
subfield: SNARG and SNARK foundations
open: Can we construct standard-model succinct non-interactive arguments (SNARGs) for all of NP with fully adaptive soundness, assuming only ordinary polynomially hard LWE?
status: The current best is the 2026 non-black-box result of Jin–Lu–Peng, *SNARKs from LWE via Non-black-Box Reductions* (DOI: 10.1145/3798129.3800888), which achieves its guarantees only with qualifications: the language class is UP rather than NP, and both provability and soundness come with caveats.
solved_when: A construction is given for all NP with fully adaptive soundness in the standard model, from plain LWE alone, with no additional qualifications (such as restricting to UP, or relying on provability/soundness caveats).
why: It would ground general succinct verification in a conventional post-quantum assumption.
key_works: Jin–Lu–Peng (2026), *SNARKs from LWE via Non-black-Box Reductions*, DOI: 10.1145/3798129.3800888.

title: Public-coin diO without knowledge assumptions
subfield: Stronger obfuscation notions, auxiliary information, and leakage
open: Can public-coin differing-inputs obfuscation be constructed from indistinguishability obfuscation together only with conventional assumptions, without invoking KOALA or any other knowledge-style assumption? Formally, the goal is a construction of public-coin diO from iO and standard assumptions.
status: As of an October 2026 preprint, public-coin diO is known from KOALA and iO (Chen–Vaikuntanathan, 2026, *Public-coin Differing-input Obfuscation from KOALA and iO*, ePrint 2026/2346); removing the knowledge-style assumption remains open.
solved_when: A construction of public-coin differing-inputs obfuscation is given, basing its security solely on iO and conventional assumptions, with no reliance on KOALA or any other knowledge-type assumption.
why: It would yield a stronger obfuscation primitive while avoiding assumptions about what an adversary "knows" — assumptions that are conceptually harder to justify and verify.
key_works: Chen–Vaikuntanathan (2026), *Public-coin Differing-input Obfuscation from KOALA and iO*, ePrint 2026/2346.

why: It probes a major unresolved boundary of what iO implies.

title: Optimal post-quantum threshold tracing without a ramp
subfield: Traitor tracing and accountable broadcast
open: Can one build threshold traitor tracing whose parameters depend only polylogarithmically on the number of users, while supporting ordinary (non-ramp) thresholds and resting solely on the plain LWE assumption?
status: The known optimal classical parameters rely on pairings; the lattice-based candidate (Das–Datta–Partap–Sasmal–Zhandry, *Optimal Threshold Traitor Tracing*, ePrint 2025/2154) requires special secret sharing and ramp thresholds rather than ordinary thresholds.
solved_when: A threshold tracing scheme is given with polylogarithmic dependence on the user count, ordinary thresholds, and a proof of security from plain LWE alone.
why: It would combine compact accountability for broadcast content with post-quantum security, something currently achievable only classically via pairings.
key_works: Das–Datta–Partap–Sasmal–Zhandry (2025/2026), *Optimal Threshold Traitor Tracing*, ePrint 2025/2154.

title: Optimal key cost for many-message statistical uncloneability
subfield: Uncloneable encryption, quantum money, and one-shot capabilities
open: How does the cost of statistically uncloneable encryption grow, or fail to grow, when the same key protects many ciphertexts rather than a single message? In other words, characterize secure key amortization and recycling across many ciphertexts, together with matching lower bounds against adversaries who attack the ciphertexts jointly.
status: Existing one-time arbitrary-message security does not settle the many-message resource frontier (see Bhattacharyya–Broadbent–Culf, 2026, arXiv:2607.28561).
solved_when: A characterization of the key cost for many-message statistical uncloneability is established, with a scheme achieving amortized/recycled key cost matching a proven lower bound under joint (multi-ciphertext) attacks.
why: It would distinguish genuinely reusable protection from repeated one-time key provisioning, settling the true resource frontier for uncloneable encryption across many messages.
key_works: Bhattacharyya–Broadbent–Culf (2026), arXiv:2607.28561.

title: Witness encryption from plain LWE
subfield: Witness encryption and conditional release
open: Can we build witness encryption for NP from plain LWE alone, avoiding indistinguishability obfuscation, evasive-lattice assumptions, and idealized group models? Formally: a construction whose security reduces to standard (plain) LWE in the standard model.
status: Recent generic-group constructions — Hair–Sahai (2026), *Witness Encryption via Prime-Order Generic Groups*, arXiv:2609.18275, and Jin (2026), *Witness Encryption for NP from SNARGs and Groups*, ePrint 2026/2063 — open a different route but do not settle this standard-model lattice target.
solved_when: A witness encryption scheme for NP is constructed and proven secure under a reduction from ordinary LWE, with no reliance on general iO, evasive assumptions, or idealized/generic groups.
why: It would let any efficiently verifiable piece of evidence serve as the condition for releasing a decryption, making encryption contingent on arbitrary NP witnesses.
key_works: Hair–Sahai (2026), *Witness Encryption via Prime-Order Generic Groups*, arXiv:2609.18275; Jin (2026), *Witness Encryption for NP from SNARGs and Groups*, ePrint 2026/2063.
